Domyn Agents is a Python library for building AI agents: agents that call tools, hand work to each other, and work with any LLM provider. It also ships a command-line assistant built with the library, so you can work with an agent in your terminal without writing any code.

From the terminal. domyn run opens a chat with an agent that reads and edits the files of a directory and runs commands in it, asking before it changes anything. You configure it with a setup wizard and extend it with skills and standing instructions. Start with the CLI quickstart. As a library. Build your own agents in Python or YAML, give them your tools, put them in teams, and run them from your application. Start with the library quickstart. The two meet: an agent you build can be opened in the terminal with domyn run agent.py, and the terminal assistant is an ordinary agent configuration you can change.

Agents. An agent has a name, a description, an instruction (its system prompt), an LLM provider and tools. Agents can form a team: a main agent hands work to the members whose description fits, and continues with what they return. See Orchestration. Tools. Tools are how an agent acts. Any Python function can be one; tools can also stream their output, or come from a remote MCP server. See Tools. LLM providers. A provider connects an agent to a model: the models of your Domyn platform space, OpenAI, Anthropic, vLLM, Cerebras, OpenRouter or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or one you write. See LLM providers. Planner strategies. A planner runs an agent's turn as a loop: reason, call a tool or another agent, read the result, repeat until it can answer. See Planner strategies. Runner and events. The Runner executes an agent and yields an event for every step: each model call, tool call, hand-off and reply. An application shows an agent to its users by reading these events. See Events and streaming.

The setup wizard saves the session's configuration to ~/.domyn/config.yaml. Run domyn setup to go through the wizard again, use /model to change only the model, and /config to see what a session runs on.

domyn setup asks, in this order: Part What it asks Model The provider, the model, the URL, the API key, the maximum tokens of a reply and the context window. For domyn, also the space id and the configuration id, and the model is picked from the models of the space. See the CLI quickstart. Instructions The agent's name (empty: Assistant, at most 30 characters), then a folder or file holding your SOUL.md / AGENTS.md, then whether to also load them from ./.domyn and ./.agents in the folder the session starts in, then extra instructions for the agent, the start of its system prompt (empty: none). See Standing instructions. Tools A checklist of the built-in tools: files, shell and browser, all ticked the first time. Untick them all for an agent that only talks. Skills A checklist of the built-in skills, by group, all ticked the first time; then a folder of your own skills; then whether to load skills from ./.domyn/skills and ./.agents/skills in the folder the session starts in. See Skills. Run again over an existing configuration, the wizard first shows each part as it is and asks whether to keep it; Enter keeps it and skips its questions. In a part you do not keep, each field opens with its saved value: Enter keeps it, and erasing it gives back the default the question names, such as the provider's own URL or the last released configuration. Keeping the skills does not reinstall the built-in ones, so a built-in skill changed by an upgrade arrives only when you do not keep them. On a terminal, Ctrl-B goes back to the previous question, which opens on the answer you gave it. Ctrl-C stops the wizard and saves nothing. Renaming the agent changes which past messages it recognizes as its own: in a conversation started under the old name, resumed with --resume or still open, the model no longer sees its earlier replies and tool results, only your messages.

The file is an ordinary YAML configuration, so anything you can declare there you can declare here, such as more agents, MCP servers or hooks. The wizard writes something like this: version: '1.0' entrypoint: Assistant llm_providers: - name: default_provider type: openai model_name: gpt-4o generation_params: max_tokens: 16000 planner_strategies: - name: tool_use_thought type: tool_use_thought compactor: strategy: two_phase agents: - name: Assistant description: A general-purpose assistant instruction: You are a helpful assistant. Be concise and accurate. llm_provider: default_provider planner_strategy: tool_use_thought stream: true skills: source: type: local_dir paths: - .domyn/skills - .agents/skills - /home/me/.domyn/builtin-skills/productivity/brainstorming standing_instructions: source: type: local_dir paths: - /home/me/notes/SOUL.md - .domyn - .agents tool_bundles: - cli_tools tool_bundles: - name: cli_tools bundles: - files - shell - browser workspace: null sandbox: local isolate_environment: true allowed_env: [] The relative paths are the folders the wizard loads from the directory the session starts in, when you answered yes to them; the absolute ones are the files and skills it found or installed. The settings you are most likely to change: Setting What it does context_window The model's context window, in tokens. Left out (auto in the wizard), the session asks the provider at start and assumes 150,000 when it cannot answer; /context shows the window it got. Set it when the provider reports none, or a wrong one: the session compacts the conversation based on it. stream true prints the answer as it is generated, false when it is complete. bundles The built-in tools: files, shell and browser. Remove one to take those tools away, or leave the list empty for an agent that only talks. skills The skills the agent loads. Only what is listed here is loaded. standing_instructions The standing instructions added to the system prompt on every turn. workspace The directory the file tools are confined to. null means the directory the session starts from. isolate_environment false lets commands use the environment you run domyn from instead of a virtual environment per conversation. allowed_env Names of environment variables that commands may see. compactor.strategy How the conversation is shortened: two_phase (default), prune_only (never calls the model) or noop (never shortens).

With browser in bundles, its options go in a browser block on the same entry. Every key is optional: tool_bundles: - name: cli_tools bundles: - files - shell - browser browser: allowed_domains: - github.com - docs.python.org allow_private_urls: true Option What it does allowed_domains The only sites the browser may contact, the requests a page makes included. Empty (the default) means any public site. allow_private_urls true lets the browser open addresses on your machine or your network, such as a dev server on localhost. Default false. engine chrome (default) or lightpanda, a much lighter browser that renders nothing, installed separately. executable_path The browser to launch, for Lightpanda when it is not on your PATH. cdp_url Drive a browser that is already running, over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, instead of launching one. It cannot be combined with allowed_domains. headed true shows the browser window. idle_timeout_s Seconds without a browser command before the browser closes itself. Default 300; 0 keeps it open. command_timeout_s The longest one browser command may take, page load included. Default 60. An unknown key in this block is refused rather than ignored, so a misspelt allowed_domains cannot leave the browser unfenced. API keys are never written to this file. See Installation for where they are read from.

A project is a separate configuration, kept side by side with the default one: its own model and API key, tools, skills, standing instructions, approvals and conversation history. Use one to switch between two setups, say one for work and one for personal use, or to share a setup with someone else. Command What it does domyn setup --project work Creates the project work in ~/.domyn/projects/work with the setup wizard, or changes it if it exists. domyn run --project work Starts a session with it. The banner shows the project's name. domyn export <folder> Saves the configuration, with the skills and instruction files it uses, into a new folder: a project that works on any machine. With --project work, it exports that project. /export <folder> does the same from inside a session. domyn setup --import <folder> Creates a new project from an exported folder, named after the folder unless --project gives another name. The wizard shows each exported setting and asks whether to keep it. --project also takes the path of a project folder anywhere on disk: anything containing / or starting with . or ~, such as --project ./shared. An export also holds a hidden .info file saying what made it: the version of domyn-agents, the date, the Python version and the platform, and the version of domyn-platform-sdk when it is installed. Nothing in it names your machine or you. domyn setup --import compares that version with its own and, when they differ or the export does not say, prints a warning before the wizard. The import goes on either way, but the exported configuration and built-in skills are as that version wrote them. When you choose not to keep the exported skills during an import, the wizard lists them, ticked, and below them, unticked, the built-in skills the export does not include, so you can add any of them. The built-ins you tick are installed into the project's builtin-skills folder; the exported ones stay as they came, edits included. To replace them with this version's, run domyn setup --project <name> afterwards. A project reads nothing from ~/.domyn except API keys: a key is read from the project's own credentials file first, then from ~/.domyn/credentials, so a key saved once serves every project, and a project can use a different one by setting its own. Its conversations and approvals are its own. An export names nothing outside its own folder: the files the configuration reads (skills, instruction files, the code of tools and hooks) are copied in, and a path that cannot be, such as a tool bundle's workspace, refuses the export, saying which. domyn setup --import refuses an export that names anything outside itself, so an edited export cannot make your machine read a file of yours. A project used by its path (--project ./folder) is checked every time: if it names files outside its folder, domyn lists them and asks before using it, and domyn run also shows the code of its tools and hooks, with what each imports, and asks before running it. Without a terminal to ask on, such a project is refused. A project used by name (--project <name>, a folder under ~/.domyn/projects that setup made or imported) is trusted and used as it is. An export never includes API keys, approvals or conversation history: when the configuration needs a key, the export says which environment variable to set.

/voice transcribes on your machine by default. A voice block, at the top level of the file beside the agent, changes how: its transcriber takes the same fields as any transcriber. voice: transcriber: type: local language: it # detected when left out; Parakeet always detects it To transcribe on a server instead, such as a speech model served by vLLM: voice: transcriber: type: openai url: http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions model: openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo api_key_env: ASR_API_KEY The setting is read when voice is turned on, so a change takes effect at the next /voice in a new session.

Path What it holds config.yaml The session's configuration credentials API keys pasted into the wizard, readable only by you conversations.db Every saved conversation approvals.yaml Approvals that last "always" projects/ Your projects, and approvals that last for one project builtin-skills/ The built-in skills you chose in domyn setup, copied from the package. Every domyn setup deletes and rewrites it, so keep your own skills elsewhere, such as ./.domyn/skills models/ The speech model /voice downloads the first time ~/.domyn is not a folder for standing instructions: a SOUL.md or AGENTS.md there is not read, unless you give its path to domyn setup.

domyn run opens a chat session with an agent in your terminal. The agent can read files, edit them and run commands in the directory you start it from, and it asks before doing anything that changes something. To try it for the first time, start with the CLI quickstart.

Command What it opens domyn run A session with the agent configured in ~/.domyn/config.yaml. The first time, the setup wizard runs before it. domyn run "<message>" The same session, with <message> sent as the first message. domyn run agent.py A session with the agent defined in a Python file. domyn run agent.yaml A session with the agent defined in a YAML file. domyn run --project <name> A session with a project: a separate configuration with its own model, keys, skills and history. domyn run --resume <conversation_id> A past conversation, to continue it. Without an id, you pick it from a list. For a conversation started from a file, give the file too: domyn run agent.yaml --resume <conversation_id>. When a Python file defines more than one agent, domyn run picks the one that is not a sub-agent of another; if there are several such agents, it takes the first and says which. To choose a different one, pass the name of its variable with --agent-name. Other options: Option What it does --expand-skills Gives the model every skill in full up front, instead of an index it reads from on demand. Uses more of the context window. --skill-sections Lists each skill's sections in the index. Uses more of the context window. --verbose, -v Shows the internal events: model calls, hooks, agent handoffs. --no-banner Skips the startup banner. Which skills and standing instructions a session reads is not an option: it is in the configuration, and domyn setup asks about it (see Configuring the CLI).

Type a message and press Enter. To start a new line without sending, press Ctrl+J, or Alt+Enter (on a Mac, Option+Enter, if the terminal is set to use Option as Meta). The answer is printed as it is generated, together with each tool call the agent makes, one line per call. While the model is working or a tool is running, a clock shows how long that step has taken (thinking or executing), and when the turn ends the session prints its total time. The answer and the model's reasoning are rendered as Markdown: headings, lists, quotes, code blocks with syntax colours, and tables with borders. A line appears once it is complete; the line still being written, or a table still being received, is shown above the input line until it is. When the output is not a terminal that shows colour, such as a pipe, a file or a terminal with NO_COLOR set, the text is printed as the model wrote it, so output redirected to a file keeps the Markdown source. While the agent is working you can keep typing: A message is delivered to the agent at its next step, so you can correct or add to a request without waiting for the answer. A command that only shows something, such as /context or /help, runs at once, and so does /auto. Any other command, such as /clear or /model, is held and runs when the agent finishes. A held /clear clears the screen right after the answer is printed; /resume shows that conversation again. Ctrl-C depends on what is happening: When Ctrl-C The agent is working Stops the current turn. The session stays open. You have typed something Clears the line. The line is empty Shows press Ctrl-C again to quit. A second Ctrl-C within a moment ends the session. Changing the configuration needs no restart. The configuration file is read again before every message, so a change to it, made by hand, by the agent or by domyn setup in another terminal, is used from the next message, and the session says Reloaded <file>: it changed since the last message. A file that no longer loads is reported once, and the session keeps the configuration it had. Only the options given to domyn run and API keys saved in the credentials file need a restart. Skills and standing instructions are read again every turn too. When a turn adds or removes one, for example a skill the agent wrote, the session says so in a line such as Now: 4 skills (+weekly-report). Ctrl-D and /exit also end the session. When it ends, if anything was said, it prints the conversation id and the command that resumes it, which is how you get back to it.

/voice, or starting with domyn run --voice, turns on push-to-talk. It needs the audio extra, which the standalone installer already includes (with uv: uv tool install 'domyn[cli,audio]'), and a microphone; the first time, the speech model is downloaded (about 670 MB, into ~/.domyn/models) and macOS asks whether the terminal may use the microphone. Hold the space bar on an empty line and speak; let go to send. What you said is transcribed on your machine and sent as if you had typed it, so it appears as your message. Tap it instead, and recording goes on until the next tap: for a long message, or a keyboard without key repeat. During a turn, the space bar stops the agent, as Ctrl-C does, and what you say next becomes the next message. A line above the prompt says when the microphone is open (● recording), and when the transcription is running. A space in the middle of a sentence is still a space, and approvals are still answered on the keyboard. A terminal reports when a key is pressed, not when it is let go, so the release is read from the key repeat stopping: the message is sent a fraction of a second after you let go. /voice again turns it off. The language is detected from what you say; to transcribe somewhere else, or to fix the language, see Voice.

Type /help in a session for this list. Commands complete with Tab. Command What it does Session /help Lists the commands. Also /?. /exit Ends the session. Also /quit and /q. /clear Starts a new conversation and clears the screen, scrollback included. The previous one stays saved, and /resume brings it back. /resume [conversation_id] Continues a past conversation, redrawing it on a cleared screen. Without an id, shows the recent ones to pick from. /verbose Turns on or off the display of internal events and library logs /voice Turns push-to-talk on or off: hold the space bar to speak, let go to send. See Talking instead of typing. Agent and model /agent Shows the active agent, its tools, its sub-agents, the conversation id and the conversation's working directory /model Changes the provider and the model, and saves them to ~/.domyn/config.yaml. Only for a session on the saved configuration, not one started from a file. /config Shows the path and the contents of the configuration file this session runs on, without secrets. A session started from a Python file has none. /skills Lists the skills available to the agent /skill <name> Shows one skill in full /skills-autodiscover [on|off] Shows, or turns on or off, loading skills from ./.domyn/skills and ./.agents/skills of the folder domyn run started in. Saved to the configuration and used from the next message. /export <folder> Saves this session's configuration, with the skills and instruction files it uses, into a new folder: a project you can share or run elsewhere. Never includes API keys, approvals or history. Approvals /approvals Lists the approvals in force: for this conversation, this project and always. /approvals revoke <n> removes the ones you name by number, /approvals clear removes them all. /auto Turns automatic approval on or off, as Shift+Tab does. While on, every tool call runs without asking, and the prompt says so, until you turn it off or the session ends. Context /context Shows how much of the model's context window the last request used, and what used it. Empty until the first request. /compact Shortens the conversation now. The shorter version is used from the next request. Background commands /ps Lists the commands this conversation started that are still running in the background /stop <handle> Stops one of them, by the handle /ps shows

Every conversation is saved to ~/.domyn/conversations.db. /clear starts a new one without deleting the old one, and /resume or domyn run --resume brings any of them back. A resumed conversation is drawn again as it looked: your messages, the answers and the tool calls, up to the last 20 turns, with a line counting the earlier ones that are not shown. The agent still receives the whole conversation. A ── resumed here ── line marks where the new part begins. The conversation id printed when a session ends is the only way to name one directly, so keep it if you want to come back to it. A conversation started from a file is resumed with the same file, domyn run agent.yaml --resume <conversation_id>; the command printed at the end already includes it.

Every model can read only a limited amount of text at once, its context window. /context shows how much of it the conversation uses. When a conversation gets close to the limit, the session shortens it automatically: first it replaces old tool outputs with a short note saying what they were, and if that is not enough, it has the model summarize the older part of the conversation. You see when this happens. /compact replaces old tool outputs right away, without waiting for the limit. For how it works and how to change it, see Context compaction.

The agent the setup wizard configures can work in the directory you start the session from: it reads and edits files and runs commands there, and it can browse the web. This page covers what it can reach and how you stay in control of what it changes.

The setup wizard asks which sets of tools the agent gets, with all three ticked the first time. Untick one to leave it out: Set Tools Approval files read_file, list_dir, glob_files, grep Never asked: they only read write_file, append_file, edit_file Asked for every file shell run_command Asked for every command browser browser_open, browser_snapshot, browser_read, browser_scroll, browser_back Never asked: they open and read pages browser_click, browser_type, browser_press Asked for every action read_file also reads documents: PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument, RTF and EPUB files are converted to text on your machine. A PDF is read page by page. A scanned page is read from the text its scanner recognized, when the scanner left it in the file; otherwise it is not read, nor is the content of a large image, and the agent is told which pages and images were left out. An agent you run from your own file has only the tools you gave it, not these. A tool result too long to send to the model whole is cut down to its start and its end, and the agent is told how to read the rest with read_tool_result. That tool is in no set and is never asked: it only reads results already in the conversation.

The directory you start the session from is the agent's workspace. The file tools cannot reach anything outside it, even with your approval, and that includes a symbolic link inside the workspace that points outside. The one exception is the folders of the skills the agent loads, so it can read a skill's files and edit a skill when you ask; writing there still needs your approval. Your standing instructions are not part of it when they are outside the workspace. To give the agent a project, cd into it before you run domyn. Commands also start in the workspace, but a command can reach any path you could reach yourself. That is why every command asks for approval.

Their own Python environment. Each conversation gets a virtual environment under <workspace>/.domyn/conversations/<conversation_id>/venv, so a package the agent installs stays there and cannot break the environment you run domyn from. To let commands use your own environment instead, for example when the agent works on that project, set isolate_environment: false (see Configuring the CLI). Only safe environment variables. Commands see a fixed set such as PATH and HOME, not your API keys or anything loaded from .env. To pass a variable through, list its name under allowed_env.

A command that is still running after its timeout (two minutes unless the agent asks for more) is not killed. It continues in the background, and the agent gets a handle to check on it later or stop it. The agent can also start a command in the background from the outset, such as a server or a file watcher, and gets its handle at once. /ps lists these commands and /stop <handle> stops one. A command detached by the shell itself, with &, disown or setsid -f, gets no handle: it does not appear in /ps and cannot be stopped with /stop. The agent is told so when it runs one. They keep running after the session ends, and the session tells you which ones are still running when you leave.

The browser set drives a real browser through agent-browser. The standalone build of domyn includes it. Otherwise install it yourself, with npm install -g agent-browser or brew install agent-browser; the setup wizard warns you when it is not on your PATH. The first time the agent uses a browser tool and no Chrome or Chromium is found, domyn downloads Chrome for Testing (about 200 MB) into ~/.domyn/browsers/, once, and says so. A Chrome you already have is used as it is. To use another browser, set browser.executable_path. On Linux, Chrome also needs system libraries (libnss3 and a few others, or agent-browser install --with-deps). The agent opens a page, reads its text or the list of elements on it, scrolls and goes back without asking. Clicking, typing and pressing a key wait for your approval, which names the site and the element, such as https://github.com :: click 'Sign in' [@e5]. Before an approved action runs, the session checks that the browser is still on that page and that the element still has that name; if anything changed, nothing runs and the agent is told why. When the agent types into a field whose name looks like a password, a token or a card number, the approval shows how many characters it types, not the text. What the browser may open: Only http and https addresses: no local files. No address on your machine or your local network, such as localhost:3000, unless you set allow_private_urls (see Configuring the CLI). Cloud metadata addresses are refused even then. Any public site, unless you list the only ones allowed in allowed_domains. The text of a page reaches the agent marked as data from the page, not instructions. That makes a page that tries to give the agent orders easier to spot, but it is not a guarantee: the approvals above are what stop an action you did not want. Each conversation has its own browser, closed when the session ends, or after five minutes without a browser command.

When the agent wants to write a file or run a command, the session shows the call in full and asks run it?. The heading is what an approval applies to, such as $ git status for a command or write_file path=notes.md for a file; below it come the arguments it does not already show, exactly as the agent wrote them: the content of a file to write, or an edit as a diff of the lines it removes (-) and adds (+). A command on several lines is shown as written, under the name of the tool. The question comes with a numbered list of answers: choose one with the arrow keys, or type its number, and press Enter. If the agent is still working, the list appears in the input line. Choose no, or press Ctrl-C, and the agent is told the call was refused, then continues without it. The yes answers differ in how long the approval is remembered: Answer Lasts yes, just this once This call only yes, this exact call, for the rest of this conversation Until the conversation ends yes, this exact call, in this project For every session started from this directory yes, this exact call, always For every session yes, anything matching a pattern, for the rest of this conversation For the rest of this conversation A session started from your home directory offers no project choice, because your home directory is not a project. The pattern choice appears for commands and browser actions. For a command it proposes a pattern such as $ git *, which you can edit before saving; for a browser action, the whole site, such as https://github.com :: *, which covers every click, typing and key press on that site. A command made of several parts, such as git pull && make, is covered only when every part matches an approved pattern, so approving $ git * never approves git status && rm -rf build. Commands that run other commands, such as bash, sudo or xargs, never get a pattern proposed. Approvals that last beyond the conversation are saved in your home directory, never in the project: ~/.domyn/approvals.yaml for "always", and ~/.domyn/projects/ for a project. /approvals lists and removes them. /auto, or Shift+Tab, skips every approval until you turn it off the same way or the session ends. Shift+Tab works at the prompt, while the agent is working, and on an open approval question. Use it only when you trust what the agent is about to do. A short list of commands is refused even then, such as deleting your home or root directory, formatting a disk, or piping a downloaded script into a shell. That list catches accidents; it is not a security boundary. For approvals in your own agents, see Tool approvals.

Domyn Agents is published on PyPI as domyn; the GitHub repository is domyn-agents. The library requires Python 3.11 or later. The CLI can also be installed without Python, as a standalone build.

The installer downloads a build of the domyn command that carries its own Python, so it needs neither Python nor uv on your machine: curl -fsSL https://github.com/domynai/domyn-agents/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh Builds exist for macOS on Apple Silicon and for Linux on x86-64 and ARM64 with glibc 2.33 or later (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, RHEL 9 or newer). Intel Macs and musl systems such as Alpine are not supported. The installer checks the download against its published checksum, puts the runtime in ~/.local/share/domyn and the domyn command in ~/.local/bin, and adds that directory to your PATH in your shell profile if it is not there already. Open a new terminal afterwards, or reload the profile it names. Running it again replaces the installed version. Variable Default Description DOMYN_VERSION the latest release The release to install, for example 1.5.0. DOMYN_HOME ~/.local/share/domyn Where the runtime goes. DOMYN_BIN_DIR ~/.local/bin Where the domyn command goes. Set them for the sh that runs the script: curl -fsSL …/install.sh | DOMYN_VERSION=1.5.0 sh. To uninstall, delete the two paths: rm -rf ~/.local/share/domyn ~/.local/bin/domyn. Your configuration and conversations in ~/.domyn stay where they are. The standalone build is the CLI only, with the audio extra included, so /voice works without installing anything else. To use Domyn Agents as a library, add it to a project.

To install the domyn command into a Python environment of its own, install Domyn Agents as a uv tool with the cli extra: uv tool install "domyn[cli]" To install the development version from GitHub instead: uv tool install "domyn[cli] @ git+https://github.com/domynai/domyn-agents" Whichever way you installed it, check that it works: domyn --version

To use Domyn Agents as a library in your own code, add it to your project's dependencies: uv add domyn With pip: pip install "domyn[cli]" To use the development version from GitHub, add "domyn @ git+https://github.com/domynai/domyn-agents" instead, or clone the repository and run pip install "./domyn-agents[cli]".

The base package covers agents, tools, every built-in LLM provider and the CLI. Extras add the dependencies of optional integrations: Extra What it adds cli The line editor of the interactive CLI: completion, history and multi-line messages. domyn run installs it into its environment when it is missing. tracing OpenTelemetry tracing langgraph Serving a LangGraph graph through Domyn Agents, for example with domyn connect langchain LangChain and langchain-openai, to build such a graph with LangChain models slack Slack channel telegram Telegram channel audio Transcription on your machine, for voice notes and voice input (Python 3.11 to 3.14) Name several extras in one install, for example domyn[cli,tracing].

domyn connect, the platform's tools and the domyn LLM provider need domyn-platform-sdk, version 0.37.0 or later. It is not an extra: it is distributed with the Domyn platform, not on a public index, so install it next to Domyn Agents from where your platform provides it: pip install "domyn-platform-sdk>=0.37.0" Without it, or with an older one, those commands stop and give this requirement.

Each provider reads its API key from an environment variable: Provider Variable Domyn platform DOMYN_API_KEY OpenAI OPENAI_API_KEY Anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OpenRouter OPENROUTER_API_KEY Cerebras CEREBRAS_API_KEY vLLM VLLM_API_KEY Any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint LLM_API_KEY You can provide the key in three ways. When the same variable is set in more than one place, the first one in this list wins: Your shell environment, for example export OPENAI_API_KEY=.... A .env file in the directory where you run domyn, or in one of its parent directories. Every domyn command loads it automatically, so the key does not need to live in your shell profile. Keep this file out of version control. ~/.domyn/credentials, where the setup wizard saves a key you paste in. The file is readable only by you, and the key never goes into ~/.domyn/config.yaml. tip Inside a YAML configuration file, refer to a key as ${OPENAI_API_KEY} instead of writing it in the file. It is replaced with the variable's value when the file loads. See YAML configuration.

This guide takes you from a fresh install to a chat with an agent in your terminal. The agent can read and edit the files of a directory and run commands in it, asking you before it changes anything. Install the CLI before you start. On macOS (Apple Silicon) and Linux, the installer needs no Python: curl -fsSL https://github.com/domynai/domyn-agents/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh or, with uv: uv tool install "domyn[cli]" For the details of both, and for how API keys are read, see Installation.

The built-in agent can read files and run commands in the directory you start it from. For a first try, use a folder you don't mind it working in: mkdir domyn-quickstart && cd domyn-quickstart domyn run

The first time you run domyn, a setup wizard asks how to reach a model. Each field opens with its current value: press Enter to keep it, or erase it (Ctrl-U) and press Enter to go back to the default the question names (empty = …). Without a terminal, in a pipe, the value is shown in brackets and Enter keeps it. Ctrl-B goes back to the previous question. Question What to enter provider Where the model is served: domyn (the models of your Domyn platform space, the first choice), openai, anthropic, open_router, cerebras, vllm or custom (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint). model The model name, as your provider spells it. The wizard prints where to find the valid names. For domyn, when the platform URL, space and API key are known (for example from DOMYN_BASE_URL, DOMYN_SPACE_ID and DOMYN_API_KEY), it lists the models of the space for you to choose from, and an other row lets you type a name that is not listed. url Leave it empty to use the provider's default endpoint. It is required for domyn, where it is the platform's address, and for vllm and custom. space id, configuration id Only for domyn: the space whose configuration holds the model, and optionally which configuration to use (empty: the last released one). The platform URL and the space id are taken from DOMYN_BASE_URL and DOMYN_SPACE_ID when they are set: the wizard says it found them, without printing them, and Enter uses them. Type another value to replace one, and erase a saved one to go back to the variable. api key If the provider's variable (for example OPENAI_API_KEY) is already set, the wizard finds it. Otherwise paste the key, and it is saved to ~/.domyn/credentials. A key saved there appears hidden (********) when the wizard runs again or you go back to it: press Enter to keep it, or type a new one. max tokens, context window Limits for the model's replies and for its context. The defaults work for most models. agent name The name of your agent. Leave it empty for Assistant. SOUL.md / AGENTS.md A folder or file with standing instructions for your agent, and whether to load them from ./.domyn and ./.agents too. Leave the first empty if you have none. extra instructions The start of the agent's system prompt. Leave it empty if you have none. built-in tools The tools the agent gets: files, shell and browser. Keep them all ticked for this guide. skills The built-in skills to install, a folder of your own, and whether to load skills from ./.domyn/skills and ./.agents/skills. The defaults are fine. The answers are saved to ~/.domyn/config.yaml, so the wizard does not run again. Run domyn setup to change them later.

When the wizard finishes, the session opens. Create a file for the agent to work with, then ask about it: you › Create a file called notes.md with three tips for writing clear documentation The agent can read, search and list files on its own, because reading cannot damage anything. Writing a file or running a command needs your approval first, so the session shows the call and asks run it?. Choose an answer with the arrow keys, or type its number, and press Enter: yes, just this once lets it run. The other yes answers also remember the approval: for the rest of the conversation, in this project, or always. no stops it. The agent is told the call was refused and continues without it. The file tools work only inside the directory you started the session from: they cannot read or write a file outside it, even with your approval. Commands start in that directory too, but a command can reach any path you could reach yourself, which is why every command needs your approval.

Type /help to list the session commands. The ones you need first: Command What it does /help Lists every command /model Changes the provider or model /clear Starts a new conversation and clears the screen /exit Ends the session When the session ends, it prints the conversation id. To continue the conversation later, run domyn run --resume <conversation_id>, or domyn run --resume to pick it from a list. For everything else the session can do, see Sessions and commands.

This guide builds a weather agent with a single tool, in Python, and runs it.
In a Python project, add Domyn Agents as a dependency: uv add domyn

Save this as weather.py: import asyncio import os from domyn.agents import Agent from domyn.agents import BaseEvent, ExecutionEventType, Part from domyn.agents import OpenAIProvider from domyn.agents import Runner from domyn.agents import FunctionTool async def get_weather(city: str) -> str: """Get the current weather for a city.""" return f"The weather in {city} is sunny, 22°C" agent = Agent( name="WeatherAgent", description="Reports the weather", instruction="You are a weather assistant. Use the weather tool to answer.", llm_provider=OpenAIProvider(model_name="gpt-4o", api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]), tools=[FunctionTool(func=get_weather)], ) async def main() -> None: user_input = BaseEvent( event_type=ExecutionEventType.USER_INPUT, author="user", content=[Part(text="What's the weather in Rome?")], ) async for event in Runner().run( application_name="weather-app", user_id="user-1", conversation_id="conv-1", root=agent, user_input=user_input, ): if event.event_type == ExecutionEventType.RESPONSE: print("".join(part.text or "" for part in event.content or [])) if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) What each part does: The tool. Any Python function can be a tool. Its docstring is the description the model reads to decide when to call it, and its type annotations become the schema of its arguments, so write the first clearly and always add the second. The provider. OpenAIProvider connects the agent to an OpenAI model. Other providers work the same way. See LLM providers. The agent. name identifies it, description says what it does (other agents read it when they decide whether to hand work to this one), instruction is its system prompt, and tools lists what it may call. The runner. Runner().run(...) executes the agent and yields an event for every step: each model call, tool call and response. The loop prints only the final answer, the RESPONSE event.

From Python, for a single question: python weather.py Or, with the CLI installed, chat with it from the terminal: domyn run weather.py domyn run finds the agent defined in the file. The session has only the tools you gave the agent, not the file and command tools of the built-in agent.

Tools: streaming tools, MCP servers and tool hooks. Orchestration: agents that hand off work to each other. YAML configuration: the same agent defined in a YAML file. Events and streaming: every event the runner yields.

Some tools should not run just because a model decided to call them: a payment, a deletion, a message sent on someone's behalf. A tool marked with an approval_type stops the turn before it runs and waits for a person to approve or refuse the call. An approval can be remembered for the rest of the conversation or longer, and rules and hooks can decide some calls without asking.

Set approval_type on the tool: from domyn.agents import ApprovalType from domyn.agents import FunctionTool delete_tool = FunctionTool(func=delete_file, approval_type=ApprovalType.USER_CONFIRM) tools: - name: transfer type: function path: tools.py approval_type: params_update approval_type The person can USER_CONFIRM (user_confirm) Approve or refuse the call as the model made it. PARAMS_UPDATE (params_update) Also change the arguments before approving. The @tool decorator takes approval_type too: from domyn.agents import ApprovalType from domyn.agents.core.decorators import tool @tool(approval_type=ApprovalType.USER_CONFIRM) def delete_file(path: str) -> str: """Delete a file.""" ... It does not take approval_subject, approval_pattern or approval_parts (described below): a tool that needs those is built with FunctionTool. A tool without one never waits for approval: rules and hooks decide only for tools that ask for a decision.

When the model calls such a tool, the turn yields tool_start, then tool_needs_feedback, and ends. To answer, run the next turn with a TOOL_FEEDBACK event that carries the action of the tool_needs_feedback event: from domyn.agents import BaseEvent, ExecutionEventType feedback = BaseEvent( event_type=ExecutionEventType.TOOL_FEEDBACK, author="user", action=pending.action.model_copy(update={"approve": True}), ) async for event in runner.run( application_name="app", user_id="user-42", root=agent, user_input=feedback, conversation_id=conversation_id, ): ... pending is the tool_needs_feedback event. The turn continues from the tool call: Approved: the tool runs, and the stream yields its tool_end. Refused (approve=False): the tool does not run. tool_end carries a refusal as the result, which the model reads, and the agent continues without the tool. The tool_needs_feedback event carries what to show the person: Where What action.name The tool. action.parameters The arguments, as a list of name, value, type, is_required. metadata["approval_subject"] The line that describes the call, and that a remembered approval is matched on. See What an approval covers. metadata["approval_scopes"] The scopes the approval can be remembered for. See Remembering an approval. metadata["approval_pattern"] A pattern the tool proposes, to approve similar calls too, or None. metadata["approval_parts"] The parts of the call that a pattern must each cover, or None. See Patterns.

For a PARAMS_UPDATE tool, send back the parameters with new values: parameters = [ p.model_copy(update={"value": 50.0}) if p.name == "amount" else p for p in pending.action.parameters ] feedback = BaseEvent( event_type=ExecutionEventType.TOOL_FEEDBACK, author="user", action=pending.action.model_copy(update={"approve": True, "parameters": parameters}), ) The tool runs with the new values, and tool_end shows them. The edited call is checked again by the deny rules and approval hooks: an edit cannot turn a call into one that is denied. For a USER_CONFIRM tool, the parameters sent back are ignored, and the call runs as the model made it.

When the model asks for several tools at once, a call that needs approval stops the turn after the calls before it have run. The TOOL_NEEDS_FEEDBACK is about that call; the calls after it are held. Your answer runs the approved (or refused) call, then the held ones, one of which may need an answer in its turn, and only then asks the model again: it sees a result for every call it made. If a new message arrives instead of an answer, the waiting call and the held ones do not run. Each is given a result saying so, The tool … was not executed: the user sent a new message instead of answering…, so the model knows they did not happen and can ask again.

Asking for every call trains people to approve without reading. An approval can instead be remembered, by setting remember_scope in the feedback: action=pending.action.model_copy(update={"approve": True, "remember_scope": "conversation"}) Later calls that the approval covers then run without asking. Each scope is kept in a store: Scope Lasts Store once This call only. Nothing is stored. conversation The rest of this conversation. ConversationApprovalStore, in the conversation's state user Every conversation of this user. InMemoryApprovalStore (this process) or FileApprovalStore (a YAML file) A runner uses only a ConversationApprovalStore unless it is given an ApprovalPolicy with more: from pathlib import Path from domyn.agents.approvals import ( ApprovalPolicy, ConversationApprovalStore, FileApprovalStore, ) from domyn.agents import Runner runner = Runner( approval_policy=ApprovalPolicy( stores=[ ConversationApprovalStore(), FileApprovalStore(Path.home() / ".myapp" / "approvals.yaml"), ], ), ) metadata["approval_scopes"] lists the scopes that have a store, so an interface offers only those. A remember_scope with no store behind it applies to the one call. Approvals are kept per user and per agent: one user's approval never covers another user's call, and approving a call for the main agent does not approve it for a team member. Store Arguments Notes ConversationApprovalStore() Scope conversation. Kept with the conversation, so it follows it wherever the conversation is stored. InMemoryApprovalStore() Scope user. Lost when the process ends. FileApprovalStore(path, scope=ApprovalScope.USER) path: str or Path, used as given (~ is not expanded); scope: ApprovalScope, default USER A YAML file, written atomically, readable and editable by hand. One file can hold the grants of many users.

To keep approvals somewhere else, such as your application's database, subclass ApprovalStore. Its methods are async, so a store can wait on a database or a network call. This one keeps them in a SQLite table: import asyncio import sqlite3 from domyn.agents.approvals import ( ApprovalGrant, ApprovalRequest, ApprovalScope, ApprovalStore, is_already_approved, ) class SqliteApprovalStore(ApprovalStore): """Approvals that last for a user, kept in a SQLite table.""" scope = ApprovalScope.USER def __init__(self, path: str) -> None: self._db = sqlite3.connect(path, check_same_thread=False) self._db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS grants (user_id TEXT, grant TEXT)") def _rows(self, user_id: str | None) -> list[ApprovalGrant]: rows = self._db.execute("SELECT grant FROM grants WHERE user_id IS ?", (user_id,)) return [ApprovalGrant.model_validate_json(row[0]) for row in rows] async def granted(self, context=None) -> list[ApprovalGrant]: user_id = getattr(context, "user_id", None) return await asyncio.to_thread(self._rows, user_id) async def is_granted(self, request: ApprovalRequest, context=None) -> bool: grants = await asyncio.to_thread(self._rows, request.user_id) return is_already_approved(request, grants) async def store(self, grant: ApprovalGrant, request: ApprovalRequest, context=None) -> None: def insert() -> None: self._db.execute( "INSERT INTO grants VALUES (?, ?)", (request.user_id, grant.model_dump_json()) ) self._db.commit() await asyncio.to_thread(insert) async def revoke(self, grant: ApprovalGrant, context=None) -> bool: def delete() -> bool: cursor = self._db.execute( "DELETE FROM grants WHERE grant = ?", (grant.model_dump_json(),) ) self._db.commit() return cursor.rowcount > 0 return await asyncio.to_thread(delete) async def revoke_all(self, context=None) -> None: def clear() -> None: self._db.execute("DELETE FROM grants") self._db.commit() await asyncio.to_thread(clear) scope is the scope the store keeps. The runner asks is_granted before asking the person, and calls store when the person chooses to remember an approval. A store that serves many users filters by request.user_id, as this one does. Implement revoke and revoke_all too: a remembered approval must be possible to take back, and the base class only raises NotImplementedError. Pass the store to the ApprovalPolicy like the built-in ones.

An approval is remembered for the call's subject, the line in metadata["approval_subject"]. By default the subject is the tool's name followed by every argument the model sent, so a remembered approval covers only an identical call. The reasoning argument that the tool_use_thought planner adds to each call is not part of it. To make an approval cover later calls, set approval_subject. It says which arguments carry the risk, so an approval covers every call that agrees on those: FunctionTool( func=transfer, approval_type=ApprovalType.PARAMS_UPDATE, approval_subject=["account"], ) Here the subject is transfer account=IT01: approving a transfer to IT01 for the conversation approves later transfers to that account, of any amount. A function receives the arguments and returns the subject, for a value derived from them: approval_subject=lambda path, **_: f"write {path}"

To approve a family of calls, such as every file in a directory, a tool can propose a pattern with approval_pattern. It is shown in metadata["approval_pattern"], and the person can accept it, or a narrower one, by sending it as remember_pattern together with remember_scope: import posixpath write_tool = FunctionTool( func=write_file, approval_type=ApprovalType.USER_CONFIRM, approval_subject=lambda path, **_: f"write {path}", approval_pattern=lambda path, **_: f"write {posixpath.dirname(path)}/*", ) action=pending.action.model_copy(update={ "approve": True, "remember_scope": "conversation", "remember_pattern": pending.metadata["approval_pattern"], # "write src/*" }) After that, writes to src/b.py run without asking, and a write to docs/c.md still asks. A pattern is a shell-style wildcard (*, ?, […]) matched against the subject. A proposal that does not match the call it was made for is not offered. A call that does several things, such as a batch of statements, is covered by patterns only if each of its parts is. approval_parts splits the call into parts: FunctionTool( func=run_sql, approval_type=ApprovalType.USER_CONFIRM, approval_subject=["query"], approval_parts=lambda query, **_: [s.strip() for s in query.split(";") if s.strip()], ) With SELECT * approved, SELECT 2; SELECT 3 runs without asking, and SELECT 4; DROP TABLE t asks.

An ApprovalPolicy can refuse calls without asking anyone. deny_rules are patterns matched against the subject and every part; a call that matches one is refused, even if an approval covers it: ApprovalPolicy( stores=[ConversationApprovalStore()], deny_rules=["transfer account=XX*"], ) A refused call does not run. Its tool_end carries a result telling the model that an automatic rule blocked it, not the user, and metadata["denied_by"] names the rule, as deny:<rule> (deny:transfer account=XX* here). Before the deny rules, a short built-in list refuses a few catastrophic shell commands in any subject: deleting a root or home directory recursively, formatting a disk, writing to a device with dd, piping a download into a shell, and a fork bomb. It applies even to approved calls, and its refusals carry hardline:<pattern> in metadata["denied_by"]. It is a guard against accidents, not a security boundary. ApprovalPolicy(enforce_hardline=False) turns it off. ApprovalPolicy argument Type Default Description stores list[ApprovalStore] [] Where approvals are remembered, one store per scope. The runner's default policy has a ConversationApprovalStore. deny_rules list[str] [] Patterns of calls to refuse. enforce_hardline bool True Refuse the built-in list of catastrophic commands.

A PRE_TOOL_APPROVAL hook decides a call from its arguments: it returns ApprovalVerdict.allow(...) to run it without asking, ApprovalVerdict.deny(...) to refuse it, or None to leave the decision to the person. from domyn.agents.approvals import ApprovalVerdict from domyn.agents.core.decorators import hook from domyn.agents.hooks import HookPhase @hook(trigger=HookPhase.PRE_TOOL_APPROVAL) def scratch_files(tool, tool_args): if tool_args["path"].startswith("/tmp/"): return ApprovalVerdict.allow(reason="scratch files") if tool_args["path"].startswith("/etc/"): return ApprovalVerdict.deny(reason="system configuration is off limits") return None write_tool = FunctionTool( func=write_file, approval_type=ApprovalType.USER_CONFIRM, hooks=[scratch_files], ) The verdict can also be returned as {"approval": verdict}. A hook that raises has no opinion, and the person is asked. A call a hook denies carries "policy" in metadata["denied_by"]. In a YAML configuration, the hook is declared under hooks with trigger: pre_tool_approval and attached by name in the tool's hooks list, like any other tool hook. The order of the checks is fixed: the built-in list, then deny rules, then remembered approvals, then hooks (the first that allows or denies decides), and otherwise the person is asked. A deny at any step wins over an allow at a later one. See Hooks for hooks in general.

The interactive CLI asks before every file write and every command, offers to remember the approval for the conversation, the project or always, and proposes patterns for commands. /approvals lists and revokes remembered approvals, and /auto approves everything for the rest of the session.
Events and streaming: the rest of the event stream around an approval. Event types: tool_needs_feedback and tool_feedback field by field. Tools: writing the tools that need approval.

An application can be described in a YAML file instead of Python code: the model providers, the planner strategies, the tools, the hooks and the agents, each declared once and referred to by name. The file is loaded into the same objects you would build in Python, so everything on the other pages applies to agents loaded from YAML too. This page shows how a file is organized and how to run it. YAML configuration lists every key.

version: "1.0" entrypoint: Assistant llm_providers: - name: main_llm type: openai model_name: gpt-4o api_key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} planner_strategies: - name: default type: tool_use_thought max_iterations: 15 tools: - name: get_order_status type: function path: tools/orders.py agents: - name: OrderAgent description: Looks up the status of an order. instruction: Answer questions about orders using your tools. llm_provider: main_llm planner_strategy: default tools: - get_order_status - name: Assistant description: Front desk of the shop. instruction: Send order questions to OrderAgent and answer from what it found. llm_provider: main_llm planner_strategy: default sub_agents: - OrderAgent Sections are lists of named entries, and agents refer to them by name: llm_provider: main_llm, planner_strategy: default, tools: [get_order_status], sub_agents: [OrderAgent]. Order within the file does not matter: an agent can list a sub-agent declared after it. Key Description version "1.0", in quotes: an unquoted 1.0 is read as a number and rejected. Can be omitted. entrypoint The agent the user talks to. If omitted, the loader takes the last agent once agents are ordered so that each comes after its sub-agents; name it explicitly when the file has more than one top-level agent. llm_providers Model connections. See LLM providers. planner_strategies How agents reason and call tools. See Planner strategies. context_managers Custom context managers for the strategies. See Planner strategies. tools Python functions and single MCP tools. See Tools. tool_bundles The built-in file and shell tools. From the command line, domyn run opens an interactive session with the entrypoint: domyn run assistant.yaml See CLI commands. In Python, load_application_from_file returns the entrypoint agent, ready for a Runner: from domyn.agents import load_application_from_file agent = await load_application_from_file("assistant.yaml") It also connects to the MCP servers the agents use and fetches their tools. To build the agent without contacting them, load the file yourself and pass mcp_init=False: from domyn.agents.loader import load_application_from_config_new, load_from_file agent = await load_application_from_config_new(load_from_file("assistant.yaml"), mcp_init=False) Then call await agent.initialize_mcp_tools() on each agent before it needs them.

Any string in the file can contain ${NAME}, replaced with the environment variable NAME when the file is loaded: llm_providers: - name: main_llm type: vllm model_name: Qwen/Qwen3-8B url: http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions api_key: ${VLLM_API_KEY} If the variable is not set, loading stops with an error naming it, so a missing key is never sent as the literal text ${VLLM_API_KEY}. The domyn command first reads a .env file from the current directory or the nearest parent that has one, so keys can live in a file kept out of version control: # .env VLLM_API_KEY=sk-... A variable already set in the environment takes precedence over the same name in .env. In Python, load_application_from_file reads only the environment: load the .env yourself first, for example with python-dotenv.

A function tool points to a Python file: tools: - name: get_order_status type: function path: tools/orders.py name is the name of the function in that file, and it is also the name the model sees. The model reads the function's docstring as the description. path is resolved against the current directory, not against the YAML file: run from the directory the paths are written for. approval_type: user_confirm makes every call wait for a person's approval. See Tool approvals. A streaming tool, an async generator, uses type: StreamableFunctionTool with the same keys. A single tool of an MCP server: tools: - name: search type: mcp server_url: https://api.example.com/mcp name is the tool's name on the server. A tool registered in Python with @tool() can be used by name: list it in an agent's tools directly, or declare it with reference to add hooks: tools: - name: lookup_order reference: lookup_order hooks: [clean_args] The Python module that registers it must be imported before the file is loaded. The type of an entry under tools is one of function, StreamableFunctionTool and mcp, spelled exactly so. Two more exist for other uses: rest, a call to an HTTP endpoint, and delegate, a tool the model sees but that runs in another process. An entry with any other type is skipped, with a warning in the log, and the agents that list it load without it.

The built-in file and shell tools are added in bundles. Declare the bundle once and list it in each agent that should have it: tool_bundles: - name: workspace_tools bundles: [files, shell] workspace: ./project agents: - name: Coder ... tool_bundles: [workspace_tools] files adds read_file, list_dir, glob_files, grep, write_file, append_file and edit_file; shell adds run_command, check_command, list_commands and stop_command. Without bundles, both are added. The tools can reach only the workspace directory (the current directory by default), and writing files or running commands needs approval.

To give an agent every tool of an MCP server, declare the server and list it in the agent's mcp_servers: mcp_servers: - name: analytics url: https://analytics.example.com/mcp headers: Authorization: Bearer ${ANALYTICS_TOKEN} agents: - name: Analyst ... mcp_servers: [analytics] Clients connect with the classic initialize handshake (protocol_mode: legacy). Set protocol_mode: auto to let the client try the newer protocol revision first; a server that enforces Mcp-Param-* headers, such as GitHub's, then rejects calls with "header mismatch: missing Mcp-Param-... header". For a server that requires OAuth, set use_oauth: true. To choose the scopes or the client name, or to keep the tokens between runs, declare an OAuth provider and name it: oauth_providers: - name: company_sso scopes: [read, write] client_name: Support Assistant mcp_servers: - name: tickets url: https://tickets.example.com/mcp use_oauth: true oauth_provider: company_sso A named provider keeps the tokens in ~/.domyn/mcp_oauth/ by default, so the user signs in again only when they can no longer be refreshed. Without oauth_provider, the tokens are kept in memory only, and the user signs in again each time the application starts. Servers that name the same provider and share a URL share one sign-in. See Tools for what happens at sign-in.

Hooks are declared once under hooks, each with the phase it runs in (trigger), and attached by name to agents or tools: hooks: - name: log_start type: listener trigger: pre_agent_call path: hooks.py - name: clean_args type: updater trigger: pre_tool_call path: hooks.py tools: - name: get_order_status type: function path: tools/orders.py hooks: [clean_args] agents: - name: OrderAgent ... hooks: [log_start] Key Description name The function's name in path, and the name agents and tools use. path The Python file, resolved against the current directory. type listener (observes, runs concurrently) or updater (can change what it receives). trigger pre_agent_call, post_agent_call or on_agent_event for an agent; pre_tool_approval, pre_tool_call or post_tool_call for a tool. A hook registered in Python with @hook is declared with reference instead of path and type. The function's parameters depend on the phase. See Hooks.

agents: - name: OrderAgent description: Looks up the status of an order. instruction: Answer questions about orders using your tools. llm_provider: main_llm planner_strategy: default stream: true tools: [get_order_status] sub_agents: [RefundAgent] context_visibility: standard handoff_scope: explicit name, description, instruction and llm_provider are required. llm_provider and planner_strategy name entries of the file, or a provider or strategy registered in Python. An agent without planner_strategy uses tool_use_thought with its defaults. Keys that are not recognized are ignored without an error. An agent can also declare: skills, the skill directories it reads (see Skills); standing_instructions, its SOUL.md and AGENTS.md (see Standing instructions). skills: source: type: local_dir paths: [./skills] standing_instructions: source: type: local_dir paths: [./instructions] An agent that runs in another process is declared with type: delegate and a transport. See Remote agents.
