A model reads a limited amount of text per request, its context window. An agent sends the whole conversation on every model call, so a long conversation, or a few large tool outputs, eventually outgrows it, and the provider rejects the request. Compaction shortens the conversation before that happens: it replaces old tool outputs with a one-line note, and, if that is not enough, has the model summarize the older part of the conversation. When a request is rejected anyway, it compacts and sends it again. Compaction runs in the tool_use and tool_use_thought planner strategies, not in react.

Compaction needs to know the window. Set context_window on the LLM provider to declare it. Without it, the agent asks the provider before each turn: vLLM, OpenRouter, Anthropic and a gateway that publishes it report it, and for OpenAI and Cerebras, which do not, a catalogue shipped with the package has it. When nothing answers, nothing is compacted automatically until the provider rejects a request as too long (see below). The interactive CLI assumes 150,000 tokens when it cannot find out. Before each model call, the agent measures the size of the whole request: the conversation, the tool definitions, and the skills and memories added for this turn. When it exceeds the threshold, the window minus reserve_tokens (16,384 by default), the conversation is compacted first, and the shorter version is sent. The reserve leaves room for the reply. Only the conversation is compacted. The tool definitions and the turn's skills and memories count towards the threshold but are never shortened, so an agent whose tools alone take most of the window cannot get under it: the tool_definition_tokens in the llm_start event's metadata["context_usage"] says how much they take.

The estimate counts three characters per token, rounding up, plus a small allowance per message, per tool call. On its own it is off both ways: it overcounts prose, and undercounts token-dense text such as hashes, UUIDs or encoded data by more than two times. So the size is anchored to the provider's own count: each response says how many tokens its request had (usage), and the next request is that count plus an estimate of what was added since. After a compaction, the share of the difference that belongs to the text kept is carried over. What was added since the last count is only estimated, so a request that is mostly fresh, dense tool output can still be undercounted, and rejected.

The conversation is split in three parts: The head: the system prompt and the conversation's first message. Never summarized, since it frames the whole conversation. The tail: the most recent messages, about keep_recent_tokens (20,000 by default) worth, and never more than half the room the conversation has under the threshold, so that a small window can still be compacted. Never compacted, since it is what the agent is working on. The middle: everything in between, which is what gets shortened. The cut never separates a tool call from its result, which providers would reject. Compaction happens in two phases: Pruning. Each tool output before the tail longer than 200 characters is replaced with a note saying what it was, such as [fetch_report output dropped to save context — 3 lines. Read it again with read_tool_result(result_id="event_…")], with the exit code when the output had one. The agent can read the output again with that call, since the conversation keeps it whole. A sub-agent's task or report, pruned the same way, has no tool output to read and its note gives no call. It needs no model call, and in an agent conversation tool outputs are usually most of the text. Summarizing. If the conversation is still over the threshold, the agent's model is asked to summarize the middle: what the user asked for, what was established, what was tried and failed, and what is still open. The summary replaces the middle, as one message starting with [conversation summary]. The user's latest message is never summarized, wherever the tail begins. If the summary fails, the pruning is kept. The conversation itself is never rewritten: every event stays in the history. What was dropped and the summary are recorded in the conversation's state, for each agent, and applied again on every later request, so a compaction lasts and a summary is paid for once. When a later compaction summarizes again, the previous summary is part of what it summarizes.

The estimate can still fall short, or the window can be unknown. When the provider rejects a request because the prompt is too long, the agent compacts the conversation to about half its estimated size and sends the request again. It does this once per turn: a second rejection ends the turn with an error_occurred event. When the rejection states the window, as vLLM, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Anthropic and LiteLLM's do (maximum context length is 32768 tokens), that window is used for the requests that follow, and remembered for the same endpoint and model until the process exits. This needs no context_window. It works with every provider: a rejection is recognized by its HTTP status, 400 or 413, and by the provider's wording, such as maximum context length or prompt is too long. Any other error is not retried. With the noop strategy, or with compaction disabled, nothing is retried.
documents.s: When the provider rejects a request

documents.t: strategy What it does two_phase Default. Prunes, and summarizes only if pruning was not enough. prune_only Prunes only, and never calls a model. A conversation whose text alone exceeds the threshold stays over it. noop Never compacts automatically. The threshold is not reported either, since it would never be acted on.

The strategy and its limits are the compactor of the planner strategy: from domyn.agents.planner_strategy import ( CompactionPolicy, Compactor, PruneOnlyCompaction, ) from domyn.agents.planner_strategy import ToolUseWithThoughtPlannerStrategy planner = ToolUseWithThoughtPlannerStrategy( compactor=Compactor( strategy=PruneOnlyCompaction(), policy=CompactionPolicy(reserve_tokens=8000, keep_recent_tokens=4000), ), ) The strategies are TwoPhaseCompaction, PruneOnlyCompaction and NoOpCompaction. TwoPhaseCompaction(llm_provider=...) sends the summaries to another model, for example a cheaper one, instead of the agent's.

In a YAML configuration, the compactor is set on the strategy entry: planner_strategies: - name: default type: tool_use_thought compactor: strategy: prune_only reserve_tokens: 8000 keep_recent_tokens: 4000 An unknown strategy name falls back to two_phase, with a warning in the log. A react strategy declared with a compactor is rejected when the file is loaded.
~/.domyn/config.yaml is a YAML configuration too: the setup wizard writes the compactor block under planner_strategies, and context_window on the provider. Edit them there.

Option Type Default Description strategy str two_phase See Strategies. In Python, the strategy of the Compactor. reserve_tokens int 16384 Room kept free below the window, for the reply. keep_recent_tokens int 20000 Size of the recent part of the conversation that is never compacted. CompactionPolicy has a few more, in Python only: Option Type Default Description enabled bool True False turns automatic compaction off. protect_first_n int 1 Messages after the system prompt that are never compacted. keep_last_user_messages int 1 The latest user messages a summary never replaces. prune_tool_results_over_chars int 200 Tool outputs at or below this length are never pruned. keep_recent_tool_results int 3 For a compaction on request: how many of the latest results it leaves alone.

To compact now rather than at the threshold, run a turn with a COMPACTION_REQUESTED event instead of a user message: from domyn.agents import BaseEvent, ExecutionEventType, Part request = BaseEvent( event_type=ExecutionEventType.COMPACTION_REQUESTED, author="user", content=[Part(text="compact")], ) async for event in runner.run(..., user_input=request, conversation_id=conversation_id): ... It drops the older tool outputs of the agent the user is talking to, and calls no model. It leaves alone the last three results (keep_recent_tool_results), counting both tool outputs and the agent_end event that closes each agent's run, so after a few turns of one tool call each, only the latest tool output is kept. It does not need a context_window, and works with every strategy, noop included. The stream is only context_compaction_start and context_compacted, whose text says how many outputs were dropped and whose metadata["tokens_saved"] says how much the next request shrinks. The request is not added to the conversation. The shorter conversation is used from the next request. In the interactive CLI, /compact sends this request, and /context shows what the last request contained: the conversation and the tool definitions, the correction the provider's count gave them, their total, the share of the window used, and how far the request is from the threshold.

An automatic compaction shows in the event stream as context_compaction_start, before the work starts, and context_compacted, when it ends. A summary takes a model call, so an interface can use them to explain the pause, and why the agent may no longer have the details of earlier turns. After a rejected request, context_compaction_start carries rejected: true in its metadata. context_compacted reports two different things in its metadata: changed, whether anything was dropped or summarized, and sufficient, whether the result is under the threshold. A compaction can change a lot and still not be sufficient: with prune_only, a conversation whose text alone is over the threshold reports changed: false, sufficient: false on every request. Every llm_start also carries metadata["context_usage"], the measurement of the request about to be sent. Event types lists the fields of all three.
LLM providers: setting context_window. Planner strategies: the strategies that compact, and their other options. Conversations and memory: where the conversation and its state are kept.

An agent keeps three kinds of information between one message and the next: What it holds Lasts The conversation Every event of every turn: messages, tool calls, replies As long as the conversation is stored Conversation state Data your tools keep for this conversation, such as a cart or a working directory As long as the conversation Long-term memory Facts about the user, such as their name or preferences Across all of the user's conversations

The Runner stores each turn in a conversation manager, keyed by application name, user id and conversation id. A turn run with the id of an existing conversation continues it: the agent's model receives the earlier turns as history. from domyn.agents.conversation_manager import SqliteConversationManager from domyn.agents import Runner runner = Runner(conversation_manager=SqliteConversationManager("conversations.db")) Manager Where conversations live InMemoryConversationManager In the process. The default when Runner() is created without one. Gone when the process stops. SqliteConversationManager(path="./conversation.db") In a SQLite file. A conversation can be continued by any runner, in any process, that opens the same file. A turn without a conversation_id starts a new conversation, and every event of the turn carries the new id (see Events and streaming). Keep it, and pass it to runner.run(..., conversation_id=...) to continue. The manager can also list and delete conversations: store = SqliteConversationManager("conversations.db") for info in await store.get_user_conversations("shop", "user-42"): print(info.conversation_id, info.updated_at, len(info.events_history)) await store.delete_conversation("shop", "user-42", conversation_id) await store.cleanup_old_conversations(older_than_days=30, application_name="shop") A ConversationInfo carries the conversation_id, application_name, user_id, the state, the events_history (every event of every turn, including the user's messages) and created_at / updated_at.

On each model call, the agent receives the conversation's earlier turns as history, then the current turn. In a team, what each agent sees of the history is set by its context_visibility. A long conversation is shortened before it outgrows the model's context window by context compaction.
The interactive CLI stores every session in ~/.domyn/conversations.db with a SqliteConversationManager. domyn run --resume and /resume continue one.

Each conversation has a state: a dictionary that is saved with the conversation and given back on every later turn. Use it for data a tool needs again later in the same conversation. A tool receives the state by declaring a parameter named state. The parameter is not shown to the model. The tool gets a copy: to change the state, return a ToolResult with the new state, which replaces the old one, so return all of it: from domyn.agents.tools import ToolResult from domyn.agents import FunctionTool def add_to_cart(item: str, state: dict) -> ToolResult: """Add an item to the user's cart. Args: item: The product to add. """ cart = [*state.get("cart", []), item] return ToolResult( success=True, data=f"Cart: {', '.join(cart)}", state={**state, "cart": cart}, ) tool = FunctionTool(func=add_to_cart) data is the result the model reads. With a SqliteConversationManager, a turn that adds apples and a later turn, in another process, that adds pears return Cart: apples, pears. The runner keeps its own entries in the state too, for context compaction, which is why the example copies the existing state rather than starting from an empty one. A tool can also declare conversation_id, to keep its own data per conversation outside the state.

Long-term memory keeps facts about a user and gives them to the agent in every later conversation with that user. It is enabled per agent with a memory_manager: from domyn.agents.memory.managers import FilesystemMemoryManager, MemoryExecutionMode agent = Agent( ..., memory_manager=FilesystemMemoryManager( file_path="memories.jsonl", execution_mode=MemoryExecutionMode.AGENTIC, ), ) In YAML: agents: - name: Assistant ... memory_manager: type: filesystem file_path: memories.jsonl execution_mode: agentic FilesystemMemoryManager appends each memory as a line of JSON to file_path, with the user id, the agent name and the time.

Before each model call, the agent's most recent memories about the user (up to recency_limit) are added to the request, as one message right after the system prompt. They are the memories the agent stored itself, or that its direct sub-agents stored.

With execution_mode set to agentic, the agent gets a remember tool, which its model calls with a fact to keep, such as "The user prefers metric units". The memory is stored under run_config["user_id"], so pass it to the runner: runner.run(..., user_id="user-42", run_config={"user_id": "user-42"}) Without it, remember answers that the memory was not stored.

Option Type Default Description file_path str local_memory.jsonl The file memories are written to. execution_mode MemoryExecutionMode Set it to agentic: the agent decides what to store. See Storing. recency_limit int 5 How many memories, the most recent first, are given to the agent.

memories = await manager.recall_memories(user_id="user-42", recency_limit=20) await manager.delete_memory(memories[0].id) await manager.reset_memory(user_id="user-42") Each Memory has an id, the memory text, user_id, agent_name and timestamp. reset_memory can be limited to one agent with agent_name.
Context compaction: how a long conversation is kept within the model's context window. Events and streaming: the events a turn adds to the conversation. Tools: writing the tools that use the state.

Several things an agent does in a turn are not writing problems: whether a tool call is safe enough to run without asking, which skills are worth reading, which old tool output can be dropped first. Each is a fixed rule or a question put to you. A decision model answers typed questions with probabilities instead of text, in roughly 150 milliseconds. It does not generate prose. You give it a state and a set of questions, and it returns a number for each, in a single pass. Two exist: Jev (TypeSafe) and Clef (Cloudflare, which speaks Jev's API on purpose). The number is the point. A model that says "allow" tells you nothing about how sure it is; one that says 0.53 tells you to ask a person. It is off unless you configure it An agent with no decision model behaves exactly as it does today — nothing is asked, nothing is logged per turn, and no code path exists that only runs when a model is present. Configuring a provider switches nothing on by itself: every use case starts at off.

domyn setup asks. Four levels, in order of what they hand over: level what it does no no decision model shadow ask and record, change nothing active pick skills and conditional instructions; the approval gate still only records active, approvals too also let it allow or deny a tool call The approval gate is a level of its own on purpose. Everywhere else a wrong answer changes what the model is shown and the turn carries on; at the gate, allowing removes a human confirmation. The wizard asks for the endpoint and the model name, then sends a real request to check both. A failure warns and saves anyway — the endpoint may come up later. decision model: 1) no — no decision model 2) shadow — ask and record, change nothing * 3) active — pick skills and instructions; the approval gate only records 4) active, approvals too — also let it allow or deny a tool call decision endpoint [http://localhost:28080]: decision model name [Cloudflare/clef]: endpoint: answering

The wizard writes this, and you can write more of it by hand: decision_providers: - name: local_clef type: system_one base_url: http://localhost:28080 model: Cloudflare/clef # the name the SERVER exposes max_state_tokens: 73728 agents: - name: Assistant decisions: provider: local_clef approvals: {mode: active, min_confidence: 0.8} skills: {mode: active} instructions: {mode: active} tools: {mode: off} context_ladder: {mode: off} sensitivity: {mode: active, on_unknown: block} model is the name the server exposes A server that serves Cloudflare/clef rejects clef with a 404 naming the one it does serve. The name is configuration and is never derived, because the short form is the one people try first. /model and re-running domyn setup keep what you wrote by hand: the wizard replaces only the keys it asked about.

Six places, each with one direction it may move in. A name that is not in this list is refused when the config loads, so a typo cannot quietly switch on something nobody reviewed. use case what it decides it may only approvals whether a gated call still needs you allow, or deny skills which skills to read up front add instructions which ## sections apply remove, on a confident no tools which tools the turn is shown hide context_ladder which old outputs compaction drops first mark for dropping sensitivity how sensitive this turn's data is refuse the turn
documents.s: Where it is allowed to matter

documents.t: Every use case is off, shadow or active, set separately. off — not asked. No request, no latency. shadow — asked and recorded, and the turn is unchanged. This is how you watch a model on your own work before trusting it. active — the answer is used, if it clears the bar. An active use case whose backend cannot produce good enough probabilities stays in shadow and says so once.

Each use case has a min_confidence and an answer below it is ignored. The default differs per use case because the cost of being wrong does. The threshold is only as good as the number it reads, so every answer also carries where that number came from: provenance meaning native a real decision model's probability logprobs derived from an ordinary LLM's token probabilities stated the LLM was asked how sure it was, and said so none no answer A use case declares the weakest provenance it will act on. Approvals declare two: allowing removes a human confirmation and needs a real probability, while denying only adds friction you can override, so it runs on the weaker bar. Why this distinction is in the product and not just in the code Measured on 13 shell commands: the decision model got 12 right, and its one wrong answer carried 0.53, against 0.83–0.98 for the right ones — so a 0.8 threshold rejects exactly the wrong one. The same test against an ordinary LLM asked to state its confidence also got 12 right, but its wrong answers sat at 0.78–0.85, above the same threshold. Same accuracy, useless number.
documents.s: Confidence, and where the number came from

documents.t: With no decision model available, type: llm points a use case at a normal provider: decision_providers: - name: fallback type: llm provider: default_provider method: logprobs # or `stated` It asks one question per request and reads the token probabilities. Expect less: on a reasoning model the probabilities describe the thinking, not the answer, so the provider reads them backwards and downgrades itself to stated rather than report a confidence it cannot see. Use it to try the shape of the thing, not to remove confirmations.

This is the use case worth understanding in detail, because it is the one that can skip a question you would otherwise be asked. The model's verdict joins the hook verdicts, in the position the approval policy already defines: hardline rules (never negotiable) deny rules a grant you already gave hooks, and the decision model ask you Two consequences follow from that ordering, and both are deliberate: A grant returns at step 3, before hooks are read, so a model can never revoke a permission you gave. The only case the model ever speaks in is the one whose answer would otherwise have been ask the user. A hardline rule still wins outright. rm -rf / is refused whatever the model says — in fact, with a decision model configured it is refused at step 1 and the model's opinion is never reached.

sensitivity is the one use case that does not fall back to today's behaviour, because here today's behaviour is "send it anyway". A provider declares the highest level it may receive: llm_providers: - name: a_cloud_model type: openai model_name: gpt-4o max_sensitivity: internal Each turn is rated public, internal, confidential or regulated, and one rated above the ceiling is refused before the agent produces anything. A provider that declares no ceiling is never checked, never asked, and costs nothing. Because a guardrail that fails open is not a guardrail, an unobtainable rating blocks. on_unknown: allow is available and sits in the file where a reviewer can see it. A fractional rating rounds up: a turn between internal and confidential is confidential.

A ## section in SOUL.md or AGENTS.md can say when it applies, as the first line under its heading: ## SQL migrations when: the task involves a database migration or a schema change Always check the rollback path before the forward one. Sections without a when: are unconditional. A when: further down is prose, not a directive. The section is dropped only on a confident no. Between "yes" and "no" sits it does not know, and that case keeps your text — a 0.45 is a coin flip, and deleting a line you wrote on a coin flip is the mistake this rule exists to prevent. What was left out is recorded rather than vanishing, and /config shows it.

A decision that acted prints one line in the session: decision tools 4 tool(s) hidden this turn 0.96 151ms /verbose shows the rest, including decisions that were taken in shadow and not applied. /config has a Decision Models section with each use case's mode and threshold — the threshold is what actually decides, so it is shown rather than hidden. Two use cases do not print anything: skills and sensitivity. They still work, and still log at info.

A runtime failure never breaks a turn. A timeout, a dead endpoint, a malformed answer and an oversized state all arrive as "I don't know", and the turn proceeds exactly as it would with no model at all. After repeated failures the provider stops asking until the next turn. A configuration mistake is different and raises when the config loads: an unknown provider type, an unknown use case name, a provider: nothing declares. A feature you believe you configured and which is silently off is worse than a failed start. One timeout matters more than the others The approval phase has no timeout of its own, so the provider's timeout_s is the only thing between a hung endpoint and a hung turn. The default is deliberately short.

A turn of an agent is a stream of events. The Runner executes the agent and yields an event for each step: the agent starting, each model call, each tool call and its result, each hand-off in a team, and the reply. An interface that shows an agent to a user — a web app, a chat bot, the interactive CLI — is a loop over these events. This page shows how to read that stream. Event types lists every type with its fields.

import asyncio from domyn.agents import BaseEvent, ExecutionEventType, Part from domyn.agents import Runner runner = Runner() async def ask(agent, text: str, conversation_id: str | None = None) -> str | None: user_input = BaseEvent( event_type=ExecutionEventType.USER_INPUT, author="user", content=[Part(text=text)], ) async for event in runner.run( application_name="weather-app", user_id="user-42", root=agent, user_input=user_input, conversation_id=conversation_id, ): conversation_id = event.conversation_id match event.event_type: case ExecutionEventType.TOOL_START: print(f"[{event.author} calls {event.action.name}: {event.action.thought}]") case ExecutionEventType.RESPONSE_TOKEN | ExecutionEventType.RESPONSE: print("".join(p.text or "" for p in event.content), end="", flush=True) print() return conversation_id Argument Description application_name Name of your application. Conversations are stored per application. user_id Who is talking. Approval grants and stored conversations are kept per user. root The agent the user talks to. In a team, the main agent. user_input The message, as a USER_INPUT event. conversation_id The conversation to continue. Without one, the runner starts a new conversation and every event of the turn carries its id: pass it back on the next turn to continue.

An agent with one tool, asked about the weather, produces these events: event_type author What it carries agent_start Assistant The user's message, as content and as the task in action.parameters llm_start Assistant llm_end Assistant tool_start Assistant action: get_weather, parameters={'city': 'Rome', 'reasoning': 'Need the weather.'}, thought='Need the weather.' tool_end Assistant The same action, with observation='Sunny in Rome' llm_start Assistant llm_end Assistant response Assistant content: It is sunny in Rome. agent_end Assistant With the default tool_use_thought planner, action.parameters also holds the reasoning argument the planner adds to each call, the same text as action.thought. The user's own message is not yielded: the stream starts with agent_start. The turn ends with the root agent's agent_end, or earlier when it pauses for approval, fails, or a hook stops it, in which case the last event is the hook's response.

Every event is a BaseEvent. The fields an interface uses: Field Description event_type What happened, an ExecutionEventType. author The agent the event belongs to. In a team, this is how events of different agents are told apart. content A list of Parts. A part's text is meant for the user; its thought is the agent's reasoning. action For tool and agent events, the call: name, parameters, thought (why the model made it), call_id, and on tool_end the observation, the result the model reads. is_partial True for a piece of a longer output that more pieces will follow. error_code, error_message Set on errors. metadata Extra data, depending on the type: token counts on llm_start, the approval subject on tool_needs_feedback. conversation_id, turn_id, interaction_id, event_id, timestamp Identifiers, for storing or correlating events.

Most interfaces handle a handful of types and ignore the rest: Show Events The reply response_token while it streams; response when it does not stream, and for text a tool streams (is_partial) That the agent is working llm_start and llm_end Tool calls tool_start (with action.thought), then tool_end with the result, or tool_error Progress of a long tool tool_update (see streaming tools) Hand-offs in a team agent_call, then the other agent's events, ending with its agent_end A request for approval tool_needs_feedback A failure error_occurred Rendering both response_token and response never shows a reply twice: a streamed reply is not repeated as a response.
documents.s: Showing a turn to a user

documents.t: Agent.stream decides how the reply arrives. It is False by default; the interactive CLI turns it on. stream=False: the reply is one response event. stream=True: the reply arrives as response_token events, each carrying the next piece in content, as the model produces it. No response follows. So an interface that only handles response shows nothing for a streaming agent. Handle both. With streaming on, response is still emitted for replies that were not streamed: a reply the agent forwards unchanged from a tool or a team member (FORWARD_VERBATIM, see Orchestration), marked with forward_verbatim in metadata; the message of a hook that stops the turn (see Hooks); a reply that asks the user a question and waits for the answer (need_feedback set on the event). A provider streams only if it implements generate_streaming, which all built-in providers do.

When the main agent hands off, the stream shows agent_call from the main agent (with the task in action.parameters and the reason in action.thought), then agent_start and the events of the team member, with its name as author. Its answer arrives as its agent_end, with the answer in content, and the main agent continues. A team member's answer is never streamed and never a response, even when its stream is on: it is addressed to the main agent, not to the user. What the user should read is the main agent's reply.

A tool that needs a person's approval stops the turn: the stream yields tool_start, then tool_needs_feedback, and ends. The action of that event is the pending call, and metadata["approval_subject"] describes what is being approved. To answer, run the next turn with a TOOL_FEEDBACK event instead of a user message, carrying the action of the tool_needs_feedback event (pending below) with approve set: feedback = BaseEvent( event_type=ExecutionEventType.TOOL_FEEDBACK, author="user", action=pending.action.model_copy(update={"approve": True}), ) async for event in runner.run(..., user_input=feedback, conversation_id=conversation_id): ... The stream continues from tool_end: with the tool's result when approved, or with a refusal as the result when not, which the model reads and answers. Tool approvals covers who is asked, and how a grant can last beyond one call.

Event Meaning The turn tool_error A tool raised. error_code is the exception type, and the message is the result the model reads. Continues: the model sees the error and decides what to do. hook_error A hook raised, or returned something its phase does not accept. error_code is the exception type. For an agent or event hook: stops, with a generic message as a response, unless the hook was declared with break_on_error=False. For a tool hook: continues, and the call runs as if the hook had not. See Hooks. error_occurred The agent could not continue, for example because the model's API failed. error_message says why. Ends: it is the last event.

When a conversation approaches the model's context window, or the provider rejects a request as too long, the agent shortens it before calling the model, and the stream shows context_compaction_start and context_compacted around it, with token counts in metadata. An interface can show them to explain a pause, and why the agent may no longer remember details from early in the conversation. See Context compaction.
Event types: every type, when it is emitted and what it carries. Tool approvals: the approval round trip. Conversations and memory: what is kept between turns.

A hook is a function the runner calls at a fixed point of a turn: when an agent starts or finishes, before or after a tool runs, or on each event of an agent. Hooks are how you add logging, guardrails and rewrites without changing the agent: a hook can observe what happens, change the arguments of a tool call or its result, rewrite an event, or stop the turn with a message of its own.

A hook is a function decorated with @hook, with the phase it runs in as trigger: from domyn.agents.core.decorators import hook from domyn.agents.hooks import HookPhase @hook(trigger=HookPhase.PRE_TOOL_CALL) def clean_args(tool, tool_args): tool_args["city"] = tool_args["city"].strip().title() return {"new_tool_args": tool_args} and is attached to the agents or tools it applies to: from domyn.agents import FunctionTool weather = FunctionTool(func=get_weather, hooks=[clean_args]) agent = Agent(..., tools=[weather], hooks=[log_start]) The function can be plain or async. Its parameter names are fixed by the phase, and checked when the hook is defined: a function missing one of them is refused. Extra parameters are allowed, for config_params.

trigger Runs Parameters Attached to PRE_AGENT_CALL Each time the agent starts in a turn, including when a main agent resumes after a team member answered context, agent an agent POST_AGENT_CALL Each time the agent stops in a turn: when it has replied, and also when it hands off to a team member context, agent an agent PRE_TOOL_APPROVAL Before the approval gate of a tool that needs approval tool, tool_args a tool PRE_TOOL_CALL Before the tool runs tool, tool_args a tool POST_TOOL_CALL After the tool returns tool, result a tool ON_AGENT_EVENT On each event of the agent event, context an agent context is the agent's InteractionContext for the turn: context.agent_input is the event that started it, context.conversation_history what came before, and context.state the conversation state. tool_args are the arguments the tool will be called with, result is the tool's ToolResult, and event is a BaseEvent (see Event types). PRE_TOOL_APPROVAL hooks decide whether a call may run without asking a person, and are covered in Tool approvals.

Kind Declared with Can change what it receives Runs Updater @hook(...), the default yes one after another, each receiving what the previous one returned Listener @hook(..., is_listener=True) no concurrently with the other listeners A listener returns nothing, or content to show (see Showing content). An updater returns the new version of what it received, as below. An agent or tool updater that returns nothing fails, like a hook that raises.

An updater PRE_AGENT_CALL or POST_AGENT_CALL hook returns the context, changed or not. To stop the turn before the agent runs, return it with break_execution and the message to show: @hook(trigger=HookPhase.PRE_AGENT_CALL) def no_passwords(context, agent): if "password" in context.agent_input.action.parameters.get("task", ""): return { "new_context": context, "break_execution": True, "emitted_content": "I can't help with passwords.", } return context The message reaches the user as a response event, also when the agent streams, and the turn ends there.

An updater PRE_TOOL_CALL hook returns {"new_tool_args": tool_args}. Besides the model's arguments, tool_args holds the values the runner passes to the tool itself, such as state, run_config and conversation_id, so change the dictionary you received and return all of it, as in clean_args above. An updater POST_TOOL_CALL hook returns the new ToolResult, or {"new_result": ...} with a ToolResult or a dictionary of its fields. The model reads the new result: @hook(trigger=HookPhase.POST_TOOL_CALL) def shout(tool, result): result.data = result.data.upper() return result A tool hook cannot stop the call.

An ON_AGENT_EVENT hook runs on the events of its agent: the input it starts from (the user's message, or the task from the agent that called it), its hand-offs, its tool calls and results, and its reply. On the main agent it also runs on its agent_end. It sees events of its own agent that are not passed to the stream: on a team member, its reply to the main agent, which reaches the stream only as the member's agent_end. It does not see the events of other agents. on_event_triggers limits it to some event types: from domyn.agents import ExecutionEventType, Part @hook(trigger=HookPhase.ON_AGENT_EVENT, on_event_triggers=[ExecutionEventType.RESPONSE]) def mask_city(event, context): parts = [Part(text=(p.text or "").replace("Rome", "[city]")) for p in event.content] return event.model_copy(update={"content": parts}) An updater returns the event to use in place of the one it received, or nothing to leave it unchanged. For an agent that streams, the reply arrives as RESPONSE_TOKEN events, so a hook that rewrites the reply must list that type, and sees one piece at a time.

A hook can add content to the stream: a listener that returns a string, or any hook that returns {"emitted_content": ...} with its other fields, puts it in the content of its hook_end event. A hook written as a generator can report progress first: each HookResult(is_update=True, emitted_content=...) it yields becomes a hook_update event. from domyn.agents.hooks import HookResult @hook(trigger=HookPhase.PRE_AGENT_CALL, is_listener=True) async def check_quota(context, agent): yield HookResult(is_update=True, emitted_content="Checking your quota...") yield HookResult(emitted_content="Quota OK")

A hook that raises, or that returns something its phase does not accept, produces a hook_error event with the exception's type as error_code. What follows depends on where it runs: Agent and event hooks: with break_on_error=True, the default, the turn stops with a generic message as the response. With break_on_error=False, the turn goes on as if the hook had not run. Tool hooks: the call goes on, with the arguments or the result the hook received. The hook_error event still carries the generic message in its content when break_on_error=True, so an interface that shows it should not present it as a refusal.

@hook argument Type Default Description trigger HookPhase required The phase. See Phases. name str the function's name The name in events (metadata["hook_name"]) and in YAML. is_listener bool False A listener instead of an updater. config_params dict {} Extra keyword arguments passed to the function on every call, for settings that are not part of the phase's parameters. on_event_triggers list of ExecutionEventType USER_INPUT, TOOL_FEEDBACK, AGENT_CALL, AGENT_START, AGENT_END, TOOL_START, TOOL_UPDATE, TOOL_NEEDS_FEEDBACK, TOOL_END, RESPONSE_TOKEN, RESPONSE ON_AGENT_EVENT only: the event types the hook runs on. input_fields list of InputFields none The fields the hook receives instead of the phase's parameters, from the REST hooks table. The function's parameters must then have those names. metadata dict {} Free-form data kept on the hook. break_on_error bool True Whether an error in an agent or event hook stops the turn. silent bool False Keeps the hook's own events out of the stored conversation. They still appear in the stream. @hook also registers the hook by its name, so a YAML configuration can use it with reference. @hook(trigger=HookPhase.PRE_TOOL_CALL, config_params={"default_country": "IT"}) def add_country(tool, tool_args, default_country): tool_args["city"] = f"{tool_args['city']}, {default_country}" return {"new_tool_args": tool_args}

Hooks are declared under hooks, from a Python file or a URL, and attached by name to agents and tools: hooks: - name: log_start type: listener trigger: pre_agent_call path: hooks.py - name: clean_args type: updater trigger: pre_tool_call path: hooks.py - name: mask_city type: updater trigger: on_agent_event path: hooks.py on_event_triggers: [response] silent: true tools: - name: get_weather type: function path: tools.py hooks: [clean_args] agents: - name: Assistant ... tools: [get_weather] hooks: [log_start, mask_city] In a file, the function is plain: the @hook decorator is not needed. break_on_error, on_event_triggers, silent and config_params are set as keys. Every key is in the YAML reference.

A hook declared with url instead of path calls an HTTP endpoint: hooks: - name: audit type: listener trigger: pre_tool_call url: https://audit.example.com/hooks/tool-call headers: Authorization: Bearer ${AUDIT_TOKEN} input_fields: [tool_name, tool_args] The runner sends a POST with a JSON body. Without input_fields, the body holds the phase's parameters, serialized (tool and tool_args, for instance), and config_params. With input_fields, it holds only the fields named: Phase input_fields available pre_agent_call, post_agent_call agent_name, agent_input (the text of the request), last_event, interaction_history, interaction_context pre_tool_approval, pre_tool_call tool_name, tool_args post_tool_call tool_name, tool_result on_agent_event current_event, last_event, interaction_history, interaction_context The endpoint answers with status 200 and a JSON object, read as a function's return value: {} for a listener, {"new_tool_args": {...}} or {"new_result": {...}} for a tool updater. Any other status is a hook error, with the status code as error_code. Key Default Description url required The endpoint. method POST The HTTP method. headers none HTTP headers sent with every call. timeout 300.0 Seconds to wait for the answer. input_fields none The fields to send, from the table above. tool_args includes the state and run_config the tool receives, so an endpoint that gets them sees the data they carry.

Every hook run is visible in the stream: hook_start before it, then hook_update for each update, and hook_end with its content, or hook_error. Each carries the hook's name in metadata["hook_name"]. See Event types.

Tool approvals: PRE_TOOL_APPROVAL hooks, and the rest of the approval gate. Events and streaming: the events an ON_AGENT_EVENT hook sees. YAML configuration: declaring hooks with the rest of an application.

An LLM provider connects an agent to a model. Every Agent has one (llm_provider), and agents in a team can each use a different one. A provider sends the conversation and the agent's tools to the model's API and returns its reply: text, tool calls, or both. Every built-in provider supports native tool calling and streaming, and talks to its API directly over HTTP, without vendor SDKs.

type Class API Default URL Key variable domyn DomynProvider The models of a Domyn platform space, through the platform the platform's address, url is required DOMYN_API_KEY openai OpenAIProvider OpenAI Responses API https://api.openai.com/v1/responses OPENAI_API_KEY anthropic AnthropicProvider Anthropic Messages API https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages ANTHROPIC_API_KEY vllm VLLMProvider OpenAI Chat Completions, as served by vLLM none, url is required none cerebras CerebrasProvider Cerebras Chat Completions https://api.cerebras.ai/v1/chat/completions CEREBRAS_API_KEY open_router OpenRouterProvider OpenRouter Chat Completions https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions OPENROUTER_API_KEY custom CustomLLMProvider Any OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint none, url is required none The key variable is read when api_key is not given. For openai and cerebras it is read once, when domyn.agents.llm is first imported, so set it before that import, or pass api_key explicitly. cerebras refuses to start without a key; openai starts and sends no key.

In Python, create the provider and pass it to the agent: import os from domyn.agents import Agent from domyn.agents import AnthropicProvider llm = AnthropicProvider( model_name="claude-sonnet-4-5", api_key=os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"], ) agent = Agent(name="Assistant", description="...", instruction="...", llm_provider=llm) The classes are importable from domyn.agents.llm. In a YAML configuration, providers are declared under llm_providers and referenced by name from each agent. Use ${VAR} for keys, so they stay out of the file: llm_providers: - name: claude type: anthropic model_name: claude-sonnet-4-5 api_key: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY} - name: local type: vllm model_name: Qwen/Qwen3-8B url: http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions context_window: 32768 generation_params: temperature: 0.2 agents: - name: Assistant llm_provider: claude ... A provider without a name is named after its model_name. The interactive CLI writes its provider to ~/.domyn/config.yaml in this same form, from the answers to domyn setup or /model.

Option Type Default Description name str the model_name Name the provider is referenced by in YAML. model_name str required The model, as the API names it. context_window int none The model's context window, in tokens. When it is not set, it is asked of the provider before each turn (the /models listing of vLLM, of OpenRouter or of a gateway that publishes it, or Anthropic's model API), or read from a catalogue shipped with the package for openai and cerebras; answers are kept for five minutes. A request the provider rejects as too long states it too, and lowers a window set too high. Context compaction compacts at a threshold only when a window is known; a rejected request is compacted and retried either way.

Option Type Default Description url str see Built-in providers API endpoint. api_key str the key variable Sent as Authorization: Bearer <key>, or as x-api-key for anthropic. For vllm it is sent only when set. generation_params dict per provider, below Request fields added to every call, such as temperature or max_tokens. The values you give are merged over the defaults, so you only list what you change. Default generation_params: type Default openai reasoning_effort: medium, service_tier: auto, store: false, temperature: 1, max_output_tokens: 4000 anthropic max_tokens: 4096 vllm temperature: 0.7, max_tokens: 2000 cerebras temperature: 0.7, max_tokens: 8000 open_router temperature: 0.7, max_tokens: 8000 openai sends temperature only for gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-5, gpt-5-mini and gpt-5-nano, and sends reasoning_effort, as the Responses API's reasoning.effort, only for o1, o1-mini, o3-mini, gpt-5, gpt-5-mini and gpt-5-nano. For any other model, both are left out of the request.

Provider Option Type Default Description vllm timeout float 300.0 Seconds to wait for the server, for slow or large models. cerebras, open_router max_retries int 3 Attempts when the API answers with an empty body. open_router reasoning_supported bool False Sends reasoning: {effort: medium}. Set it only for models that accept the parameter: others reject the request.

The models a space of the Domyn platform offers. You authenticate with your own platform API key and name the space; the platform holds the credentials of the model's provider and forwards the request. It needs the platform SDK next to Domyn Agents, version 0.37.0 or later (see Installation): without it, or with an older one, the provider stops and gives the requirement. Option Type Default Description model_name str required The model, named as the space's configuration names it, not as its provider does. url str DOMYN_BASE_URL The platform's address, with or without https://. Also read as base_url. api_key str DOMYN_API_KEY Your platform API key. space_id str DOMYN_SPACE_ID The space whose configuration holds the model. configuration_id str DOMYN_CONFIGURATION_ID, else the space's last released configuration The configuration to take the model from. generation_params, body dict {} Request fields added to every call, such as temperature or max_tokens. domyn setup lists the space's models when it can reach the platform, so you can choose the name instead of typing it. With the three variables set, a provider needs only the model: llm_providers: - name: platform type: domyn model_name: qwen3-32b context_window: 32768

For any endpoint that speaks OpenAI Chat Completions, with full control over the request. It has no api_key and no generation_params: authentication goes in headers, and request fields in body. Option Type Default Description url str required The full chat completions URL. headers dict[str, str] {} HTTP headers sent with every request, for example Authorization. body dict {} Fields added to every request body, for example temperature or max_tokens. llm_providers: - name: gateway type: custom model_name: Qwen/Qwen3-32B url: https://llm.example.com/v1/chat/completions headers: Authorization: Bearer ${GATEWAY_API_KEY} body: temperature: 0.7 max_tokens: 512

A provider is a subclass of BaseLLMProvider that implements generate and generate_streaming: import time from collections.abc import AsyncGenerator from typing import Any from domyn.agents.core.decorators import llm_provider from domyn.agents.llm import BaseLLMProvider, LLMMessage, LLMResponse @llm_provider(name="echo", model_name="echo-1", generation_params={"prefix": "echo:"}) class EchoProvider(BaseLLMProvider): type: str = "echo" supported_structured_outputs: None = None generation_params: dict[str, Any] = {} async def generate( self, messages: list[LLMMessage], structured_outputs=None, tools=None, tool_choice=None, **kwargs: Any ) -> LLMResponse: start = time.monotonic() text = f"{self.generation_params['prefix']} {messages[-1].content}" return LLMResponse( content=text, generated_tokens=len(text.split()), execution_time=time.monotonic() - start, ) async def generate_streaming( self, messages: list[LLMMessage], **kwargs: Any ) -> AsyncGenerator[LLMResponse, None]: yield await self.generate(messages, **kwargs) What the methods receive and return: messages is the conversation, as LLMMessage objects with a role (system, user, assistant, tool), content, and, for tool use, tool_calls and tool_call_id. tools, when the agent has any, is a list of tool definitions in the OpenAI Chat Completions format: {"type": "function", "function": {"name", "description", "parameters"}}. The reply is an LLMResponse: content, generated_tokens and execution_time (seconds) are required. A tool call is returned in tool_calls, as LLMToolCall(id=..., function=ToolCallFunction(name=..., arguments=<JSON string>)). usage carries the provider's token counts. Context compaction measures the next request from the prompt count (prompt_tokens, or input_tokens with any cache counts), so return it when the API gives one. reasoning_content becomes the thought of a tool_use_thought agent when a call carries none (see Planner strategies). fetch_context_window() returns the model's window, or None. By default it reads the /models listing beside an OpenAI-style url; override it for an API that says the window elsewhere. generate_streaming yields the reply in pieces, each an LLMResponse whose content is the next piece. It is used when the agent has stream enabled. Without the decorator, create an instance and pass it to the agent, as with the built-in providers. @llm_provider registers one instance instead, created on first use with the decorator's arguments, so that YAML can use it by name, either directly or through a reference that changes some of its options: llm_providers: - name: loud_echo reference: echo config_params: generation_params: prefix: "ECHO:" agents: - name: Assistant llm_provider: loud_echo # or: echo ... The module that defines the provider must be imported before the configuration is loaded. The decorator replaces the class with a function that returns that one instance: once decorated, EchoProvider(...) returns the registered provider rather than a new one, and EchoProvider cannot be used with isinstance. config_params sets any option except type, model_name, name, url and reference, and is merged into options that are dictionaries, such as generation_params.
Planner strategies: how an agent uses its provider on each step. Context compaction: what context_window drives. YAML configuration: the rest of a YAML configuration.

One agent with many tools gets harder to steer as the tools pile up. An alternative is a team: a main agent that talks to the user and hands each request to a specialist with its own instructions and tools. This page shows how to build one, and how to control what each agent sees and which agents it can call.

Give the main agent its specialists as sub_agents: from domyn.agents import Agent order_agent = Agent( name="OrderAgent", description="Retrieves information about customer orders", instruction="You help users check order status and details.", llm_provider=llm, tools=[get_order_tool, list_orders_tool], ) payment_agent = Agent( name="PaymentAgent", description="Handles payment questions and refunds", instruction="You help users with payment questions and process refunds.", llm_provider=llm, tools=[get_payment_tool, refund_tool], ) main_agent = Agent( name="CustomerService", description="Main customer service agent", instruction="You are a customer service assistant. Route each question to the right specialist.", llm_provider=llm, tools=[lookup_customer_tool], sub_agents=[order_agent, payment_agent], ) Run main_agent as usual. It is the agent the user talks to, and the only one you pass to the runner. When a user asks "Where is order 42?": The main agent's model sees each sub-agent as one more tool it can call, named after the agent and described by its description. It calls OrderAgent, and writes a task for it: the request, restated with every detail the sub-agent needs. OrderAgent starts with that task, calls its own tools, and finishes with an answer. Control returns to the main agent, which reads what OrderAgent did and found, and answers the user, or hands off again. A sub-agent's answer goes back to the agent that called it, not to the user. A sub-agent can have sub-agents of its own, to any depth. In the event stream, a handoff shows up as an AGENT_CALL from the calling agent, an AGENT_START when the sub-agent begins, and an AGENT_END when it finishes. Every event carries the name of the agent that produced it in author.

The main agent decides whom to call only from the sub-agents' names and descriptions, so write the description for that reader: Say what the agent handles, and what it does not. "Handles payment questions and refunds. Does not change orders." routes better than "Payment agent". Keep specialists distinct. Two descriptions that could both match a request make the choice a coin toss. Tell the main agent how to delegate in its instruction: for example, to send each question to the right specialist and to answer from what the specialist found.

Two settings on each agent, independent of each other, control a team: Setting Controls Default context_visibility Which other agents' work this agent reads in its history STANDARD handoff_scope Which agents this agent can hand off to EXPLICIT from domyn.agents import ContextVisibility, HandoffScope payment_agent = Agent( name="PaymentAgent", ..., context_visibility=ContextVisibility.PEERS, handoff_scope=HandoffScope.EXPLICIT, )
documents.s: What an agent sees, and whom it can call

documents.t: Value The agent reads the work of STANDARD Itself and its own sub-agents, at any depth PEERS Also its siblings (the other sub-agents of its parent) and their sub-agents GLOBAL Every agent in the tree With STANDARD, a specialist starts from the task it was given and sees nothing of what its siblings did. Use PEERS when it needs their results: a PaymentAgent that should read the order OrderAgent just looked up. Use GLOBAL for an agent that needs the whole picture, such as one that summarizes the conversation. Every agent you open up adds to its context, so widen only where it is needed.

Value The agent can hand off to EXPLICIT Exactly the agents in its sub_agents DIRECT_PEERS Its own sub-agents and its siblings, but not into a sibling's sub-agents GLOBAL Any agent in the tree, the main agent included With EXPLICIT, the shape of the tree is the shape of the conversation: work flows down and comes back up. DIRECT_PEERS lets specialists pass work sideways, for example OrderAgent handing a refund to PaymentAgent without going through the main agent. A handoff to a sibling goes to that sibling itself, never past it into its own sub-agents, so the sibling still decides how its part is done. GLOBAL makes every agent reachable, which suits a utility agent that any other may need. The two settings combine freely: an agent can read the whole tree (context_visibility=GLOBAL) and still call only its own sub-agents (handoff_scope=EXPLICIT). note Older configurations use a single handoff_visibility key. It is still accepted, and translated into the two settings above with a warning: replace it with context_visibility and handoff_scope.

Often a sub-agent's answer is already what the user should read, and having the main agent rewrite it only costs a model call and risks changing it. For that, every agent can also call FORWARD_VERBATIM: it names the result of a sub-agent or of a tool in its history, and that text becomes the agent's answer exactly as it was written. The model decides when to use it. It is told to do so only for a complete answer that reads well on its own, and not for a partial answer, a raw record or a list of ids, an answer that points to sources outside its own text, a request for a different format, length or language, or one that combines several results. To turn it off for an agent, give it a planner with forward_verbatim_enabled=False: from domyn.agents.planner_strategy import ToolUseWithThoughtPlannerStrategy main_agent = Agent( ..., planner=ToolUseWithThoughtPlannerStrategy(forward_verbatim_enabled=False), )

In a YAML configuration, declare each agent once and list sub-agents by name. The two settings are written in lowercase: version: "1.0" entrypoint: CustomerService llm_providers: - name: main_llm type: openai model_name: gpt-4o api_key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} planner_strategies: - name: planner type: tool_use_thought agents: - name: OrderAgent description: Retrieves information about customer orders instruction: You help users check order status and details. llm_provider: main_llm planner_strategy: planner - name: PaymentAgent description: Handles payment questions and refunds instruction: You help users with payment questions and refunds. llm_provider: main_llm planner_strategy: planner context_visibility: peers - name: CustomerService description: Main customer service agent instruction: Route each question to the right specialist. llm_provider: main_llm planner_strategy: planner sub_agents: - OrderAgent - PaymentAgent entrypoint names the agent the user talks to.
Remote agents: team members that run in another process, including LangGraph graphs. Events and streaming: follow a team's work event by event.

A planner strategy runs one agent's turn. On each iteration it builds the request from the conversation history (through its context manager), calls the model, and executes what the model returns: a tool call, a handoff to another agent, or a final reply. Tool results and sub-agent results are appended to the history, and the loop repeats until the model replies or max_iterations is reached. This is the ReAct loop: reason, act, observe. The three built-in strategies run the same loop and differ in how the model is asked to act.

type Class How the model calls tools Use it when tool_use_thought ToolUseWithThoughtPlannerStrategy Native tool calling, with the model's reasoning recorded before each call Default. Any model with native tool calling. tool_use ToolUsePlannerStrategy Native tool calling, without the reasoning You do not need the reasoning. Tools have no extra reasoning argument, and the system prompt is shorter by one instruction. react ReactPlannerStrategy A text format described in the system prompt, parsed from the model's reply The model, or the endpoint serving it, has no native tool calling. Reasoning. tool_use_thought adds a required reasoning argument to every tool and agent the model can call, and an instruction to the system prompt asking the model to state its reasoning before each call. The reasoning argument is recorded as the thought of the action, on the TOOL_START or AGENT_CALL event, and the interactive CLI prints it above the call. When the first call of a reply has no reasoning, its thought comes from the provider's reasoning field (reasoning_content, as with DeepSeek R1, then thinking_blocks, as with Anthropic extended thinking), and otherwise from the text the model wrote before the call. With tool_use, thought is empty. Text protocol. With react, every step must be written in the exact format the prompt describes (<thought>…</thought><action>{"name": …, "arguments": …}</action>). A reply outside the format is a step the planner cannot parse, so prefer a tool_use strategy whenever native tool calling is available.

An Agent without a planner uses ToolUseWithThoughtPlannerStrategy() with its defaults. To choose another strategy, or to change an option, pass one explicitly: from domyn.agents.planner_strategy import ToolUsePlannerStrategy agent = Agent(..., planner=ToolUsePlannerStrategy(max_iterations=15)) ReactPlannerStrategy() needs nothing more: its default context manager sends the whole history and asks the model for the <thought>/<action> text format. from domyn.agents.planner_strategy import ReactPlannerStrategy agent = Agent(..., planner=ReactPlannerStrategy()) In a YAML configuration, strategies are declared under planner_strategies and referenced by name from each agent. An agent that names none gets tool_use_thought with its defaults, so the section is needed only to choose another strategy or change an option: planner_strategies: - name: default type: tool_use_thought max_iterations: 15 - name: text_protocol type: react agents: - name: Assistant ... planner_strategy: default Several agents can reference the same strategy. In a team, each agent can use a different one.

Option Type Default Description name str the type Name the strategy is referenced by in YAML. max_iterations int 25 Maximum model calls in one turn of this agent. When reached, the agent stops and replies Reached maximum iterations (<n>). forward_verbatim_enabled bool True Offers the model the FORWARD_VERBATIM tool, which returns a previous tool or sub-agent result unchanged as the agent's reply. See Orchestration. use_stop bool False For a sub-agent. Offers two extra tools: STOP(info), which ends the agent's work and returns info to the calling agent, and ASK_USER_MISSING_INFO(text), which ends it with a request for information. The calling agent receives the question with an instruction to ask the user and call the sub-agent again.

Option Type Default Description context_manager ToolUseContextManager / ToolUseWithThoughtContextManager a new instance, with the defaults below Builds the messages and tool definitions sent to the model. compactor Compactor two_phase, reserving 16,384 tokens Shortens the conversation before a request that would not fit the model's context window. See Context compaction. parallel_tool_calls bool True Runs the calls of one model response that need no approval at the same time; False runs every call after the one before it. See Several calls at once. Context manager options: Option Type Default Description max_tool_result_chars int 20000 Maximum characters of a single tool result sent to the model. A longer result is cut keeping its start and its end, with a line saying which characters are missing, that what they contain cannot be told from the rest, and how to read them: an agent with tools of its own, or agents to hand off to, also gets a read_tool_result tool that reads a result from its history, a part that fits this limit at a time, or lists where a text occurs in it. from domyn.agents.planner_strategy import ( ToolUseWithThoughtContextManager, ) from domyn.agents.planner_strategy import ToolUseWithThoughtPlannerStrategy planner = ToolUseWithThoughtPlannerStrategy( context_manager=ToolUseWithThoughtContextManager(max_tool_result_chars=8000), ) An agent with tools of its own, or agents to hand off to, gets the read_tool_result definition with every request, about 970 characters. An agent with neither does not, so it sends no tools because of it (a vLLM server started without --enable-auto-tool-choice rejects a request with any), and its cut results do not say how to read the rest. Neither do those of an agent with a tool of its own named read_tool_result, which keeps its own. In YAML, context managers are declared under context_managers and referenced by name. The type is thought_tool_use for tool_use_thought and tool_use for tool_use: context_managers: - name: short_results type: thought_tool_use max_tool_result_chars: 8000 planner_strategies: - name: default type: tool_use_thought context_manager: short_results

Option Type Default Description context_manager ContextManager full_messages with structural_tags prompting Builds the prompt and the history, and defines the text format the model must follow. verbose bool False When the model returns no action, also emits a RESPONSE event carrying a thought that says the agent is finishing. react does not support compactor: a react strategy declared with one is rejected when it is loaded. In YAML, a context manager for react is declared under context_managers like the ones above, and needs more keys than its Python default suggests: prompting, the text format: {type: structural_tags} or {type: json_schema}. Required. For type: full_messages, narrow_non_visible_agents: true leaves out the tool results of agents this one cannot see, false keeps them. Required. For the summarizing types (old_summary, agents_summary, interactions_summary), llm_provider: the name of an entry of llm_providers, the model that writes the summaries. Required. context_managers: - name: full type: full_messages prompting: {type: structural_tags} narrow_non_visible_agents: false planner_strategies: - name: react type: react context_manager: full

A team member does not have to run in the same process as the rest of the team. It can run on another machine, belong to a service another team operates, or be a graph built with LangGraph. In the calling application it is a DelegateAgent: the main agent hands off to it like any other team member, but its turn is executed by a remote runner, and the events of that turn come back over a transport.

caller worker ┌────────────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Runner │ │ domyn connect worker.py:agent │ │ └─ DelegateAgent │ │ └─ Agent or LangGraph graph │ │ └─ transport ─────────┼──► relay ◄───┼── relay connection │ └────────────────────────────┘ channel └───────────────────────────────┘ The two sides never connect to each other. Both connect to a relay as clients, on the same channel, and the relay forwards events between them. The caller sends an AGENT_START carrying the task; the worker runs the agent and sends back its events, ending with the reply. Domyn Agents does not include a relay: you run one, or use one your infrastructure already provides. With the websocket transport and domyn connect, a relay must: accept WebSocket connections at /relay/v1/ws, with the channel in the channel-id header; forward every message a client sends to the other clients connected to the same channel; keep the recent messages of each channel, and on each new connection first send the ones after the event id in the last-event-id header, or all of them when the header is missing. The last point matters because both sides close and reopen their connection during a turn: a message sent while one of them is reconnecting must still reach it. Both sides drop the messages they have already seen, so replaying more than needed is harmless.

In a YAML configuration, a remote agent is an entry under agents with type: delegate and a transport (the provider is declared as in Orchestration): agents: - name: Specialist type: delegate description: Counts the words in a text. transport: type: websocket url: wss://relay.example.com/relay/v1/ws headers: channel-id: <channel id> - name: Assistant description: Front desk instruction: Send counting questions to Specialist. llm_provider: main_llm sub_agents: - Specialist In Python: from domyn.agents import DelegateAgent from domyn.agents.runner.websocket_transport import WebSocketTransport specialist = DelegateAgent( name="Specialist", description="Counts the words in a text.", transport=WebSocketTransport( ws_url="wss://relay.example.com/relay/v1/ws", headers={"channel-id": "<channel id>"}, ), ) assistant = Agent(..., sub_agents=[specialist]) The main agent's model sees Specialist among the agents it can call, with its description, and calls it with a task. A DelegateAgent can also be the entrypoint itself: the application then forwards each user message to the remote agent and returns its reply.
documents.s: Adding a remote agent to a team

documents.t: Every event of the remote turn is passed through, with the delegate's name as author: LLM_START and LLM_END, TOOL_START and TOOL_END for the tools the remote agent runs, and its reply. Events of the remote agent's own team members keep their own author. The caller only observes these tool calls: the remote agent runs them, except the tools declared in the delegate's own tools (see Options), which the caller runs and whose results it sends back. How the remote turn ends depends on where the delegate sits: As a team member, its final reply becomes an AGENT_END carrying the reply, and the main agent continues. The tool calls the remote agent made are in the main agent's history too, so its model sees what was done as well as the answer. As the entrypoint, its final reply is the turn's RESPONSE. If no message arrives within the transport's timeout, the remote turn ends with error_code delegate_timeout and a text saying that the delegated agent stopped responding. For a team member, this is its AGENT_END: the text goes to the main agent's model as the result of the call, and the main agent continues. As the entrypoint, it is the turn's RESPONSE. If the caller's turn is cancelled, both transports signal the remote runner to stop: they send it an AGENT_END with error_code user_cancelled. A turn that has already ended is not signalled.

Connects to the relay over WebSocket. The connection is opened for each step of the remote turn and closed after it, so no socket stays open between turns. On each connection, the transport also sends the conversation id and the last event it received, and drops any event it has already seen or that belongs to another turn. Option Type Default Description url str required Relay URL, ws:// or wss://. Python: ws_url. headers dict[str, str] {} Headers sent on every connection. channel-id selects the channel. timeout float 60.0 Seconds to wait to connect, and for each next message. ping_interval float | None 20.0 Seconds between keep-alive pings. None disables them.

Talks to the relay over HTTP: a POST opens a Server-Sent Events stream that carries the remote events, and a result for the remote agent is sent as the body of the request that reopens it. Each POST carries the channel, space and conversation as the channelId, spaceId and conversationId query parameters, and the last event received in a Last-Event-ID header. Each event in the stream must be a JSON envelope with the event under payload; an event sent bare is dropped. domyn connect speaks WebSocket only, so a relay used with sse has to serve both. Option Type Default Description url str required Relay messages endpoint, https://…. headers dict[str, str] {} channel-id selects the channel and space-id the space, sent as query parameters. Also sent as HTTP headers, unless meta is set. meta dict[str, str] the headers HTTP headers sent with every request. timeout float 60.0 Seconds to wait to connect, to send, and for the next event.

A transport is a subclass of RunnerTransport (domyn.agents.runner.transport) that implements execute(), an async generator that yields the remote events for one turn, and send_result(), which sends an event back to the remote runner. cancel() is optional: by default a cancelled turn sends nothing. Declaring a type class variable makes it available as transport.type in YAML as soon as its module is imported: import asyncio from domyn.agents import ExecutionEventType from domyn.agents.runner import RunnerTransport # One pair of queues per url: events to the remote runner, events from it. QUEUES: dict[str, tuple[asyncio.Queue, asyncio.Queue]] = {} class QueueTransport(RunnerTransport): type = "queue" def __init__(self, url: str) -> None: self.outbox, self.inbox = QUEUES.setdefault(url, (asyncio.Queue(), asyncio.Queue())) @classmethod def from_config(cls, config: dict) -> "QueueTransport": return cls(url=config["url"]) async def execute(self, agent_name, context, run_config=None): await self.outbox.put(context.agent_input) # the AGENT_START carrying the task while True: event = await self.inbox.get() yield event.model_copy(update={"author": agent_name}) if event.event_type in (ExecutionEventType.RESPONSE, ExecutionEventType.AGENT_END) and not event.is_partial: return async def send_result(self, event, conversation_id=None): await self.outbox.put(event) agents: - name: Specialist type: delegate description: Counts the words in a text. transport: type: queue url: specialist Whatever reads outbox plays the remote runner: it answers each AGENT_START by putting the remote events on inbox, ending with the reply.

Option Type Default Description name str required Name the agent is called by. description str required What the agent does. The main agent's model chooses it from this text. transport transport required See Transports. In YAML, a mapping with a type. Without one, the agent fails when it is called. tools list of tools [] Tools the remote agent may ask the caller to run. A function tool listed here is run by the caller, and its result is sent back to the remote agent. invocation_parameters JSON Schema {"task": string} The arguments the main agent's model passes when it calls this agent, in place of the default task. They reach the remote agent as the parameters of its AGENT_START. visibility isolated | scoped | trusted | global isolated Whether the caller's run_config (user id, tokens and other request data) is sent to the remote agent. Only trusted and global send it, beside the event rather than inside it. context_visibility ContextVisibility STANDARD What history the agent sees, as for any agent. handoff_scope HandoffScope EXPLICIT Which agents it may hand off to, as for any agent. hooks list of hooks [] Hooks with the pre_agent_call, post_agent_call and on_agent_event triggers.

domyn connect makes an agent available on a relay channel. It connects to the relay, waits for AGENT_START events, runs the agent for each one and sends its events back. It runs until it is stopped. note The relay's address and headers, and the platform's tools, come from the Domyn platform SDK, so domyn connect needs the platform SDK installed next to Domyn Agents. Without it, or with a version older than it needs, the command stops and names the requirement. To reach a relay of your own with no SDK, build a DomynRelayChannel(ws_url=..., headers=...) in Python instead. export DOMYN_API_KEY=<relay key> domyn connect worker.py:specialist \ --channel-id <channel id> \ --base-url relay.example.com The argument names what to serve: path/to/file.py:symbol: a variable in a file. The file's directory is not added to the import path, so a file that imports a module next to it needs the module:symbol form, or that directory on PYTHONPATH. module:symbol: a variable in an importable module. The current directory is added to the import path. path/to/file.py: the file's root agent, the one that is not a sub-agent of another. path/to/config.yaml: the entrypoint agent of a YAML configuration. What the variable holds decides how it is run: an Agent: it runs under a Runner, with its tools and its team, exactly as it would locally; a LangGraph compiled graph, or anything else with an ainvoke method: see LangGraph graphs; a function with no arguments that returns a LangGraph graph: it is called once, at startup. This works for graphs only: for an Agent, name the variable that holds the instance. Option Environment variable Default Description --channel-id DOMYN_CHANNEL_ID Channel to serve. --space-id DOMYN_SPACE_ID Space of the channel, sent to the relay in the space-id header. --configuration-id DOMYN_CONFIGURATION_ID Sent to the relay in the configuration-id header, and used when platform tools are looked up. --base-url DOMYN_BASE_URL Relay host, with an optional port. The relay is reached at wss://<host>/relay/v1/ws, or ws:// for localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1. --target Serves several channels from one process, possibly in different spaces or on different relays. Repeatable; each is channel_id=…,space_id=…,base_url=…,configuration_id=…, where only channel_id is required. space_id and base_url default to --space-id and --base-url; configuration_id defaults to --configuration-id only when the target sets no space_id. Without --target, the one channel is --channel-id. --max-concurrency 8 Turns run at the same time. Beyond that, as many more wait, and further requests are refused. --platform-tools / --no-platform-tools on when the SDK is installed, else off Attaches to the served agent every tool the platform offers that the agent does not already declare. --no-platform-tools turns it off; --platform-tools without the SDK stops and names the version it needs. --tool-refresh-interval 0 With --platform-tools, looks the platform tools up again every this many seconds. 0 does not. DOMYN_API_KEY must be set; the command stops if it is not. It is sent to the relay in the api-key header, for a relay that checks who connects.
documents.s: Serving an agent with domyn connect

documents.t: Install the langgraph extra: uv add "domyn[langgraph]" A compiled graph is served the same way. The caller sends a task (and possibly a user_request), which rarely matches the graph's input; @input_mapper converts it: from typing import Any, TypedDict from langchain_core.language_models.fake import FakeListLLM from langchain_core.tools import tool from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph from domyn.agents.integrations.langgraph import input_mapper class GraphState(TypedDict): question: str answer: str @tool def calculator(expression: str) -> str: """Evaluate a simple arithmetic expression like '2+2'.""" return str(eval(expression, {"__builtins__": {}}, {})) _llm = FakeListLLM(responses=["It's probably 42."]) def answer(state: GraphState) -> GraphState: q = state["question"] if any(op in q for op in "+-*/"): return {"question": q, "answer": calculator.invoke({"expression": q})} return {"question": q, "answer": str(_llm.invoke(q))} @input_mapper(lambda d: GraphState(question=d.get("task", ""), answer="")) def build_graph() -> Any: builder = StateGraph(GraphState) builder.add_node("answer", answer) builder.add_edge(START, "answer") builder.add_edge("answer", END) return builder.compile() graph = build_graph() domyn connect graph.py:graph --channel-id <channel id> --base-url relay.example.com @input_mapper can decorate the factory or the compiled graph, so both graph.py:graph and graph.py:build_graph find it. Without it, the parameters are passed to the graph as they are. The graph's model and tool calls reach the caller as LLM_START, LLM_END, TOOL_START and TOOL_END events. The reply is taken from the graph's final state: the text of the last message in messages; otherwise result, if it is text; otherwise the whole state as JSON.
